Apply glucose gel to the buccal mucosa without swallowing and retest in 20 minutes
Give 250 mL of 2% milk with peanut butter crackers and recheck glucose in 30 minutes
Administer 1 mg of glucagon subcutaneously and turn the patient onto their left side
items.rationale: For a conscious patient with hypoglycemia (< 4 mmol/L), Diabetes Canada recommends 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (4 glucose tablets, 3 sugar packets dissolved in water, 175 mL regular soft drink or juice, 8 Life Savers, 1 package Rockets, or 15 mL honey), followed by retesting in 15 minutes and retreating with 15 g if still < 4 mmol/L. Milk and glucose gel act much more slowly.

items.prompt: A nurse finds a patient with type 1 diabetes unresponsive and diaphoretic in a long-term care facility. Capillary blood glucose is 2.1 mmol/L, and the patient has no intravenous access. After administering subcutaneous glucagon, what is the priority nursing action?
options: Turn the patient onto their side to prevent aspiration if vomiting occurs
Place the patient in high Fowler's position and administer oral glucose gel
Maintain a supine position and repeat the glucagon injection in 5 minutes
Elevate the lower extremities and apply warm blankets to reverse diaphoresis
items.rationale: Glucagon is given subcutaneously (or IM) to treat severe hypoglycemia in an unconscious patient without IV access. Because glucagon commonly induces nausea and vomiting, the unconscious patient must be turned onto their side to protect the airway and prevent aspiration.

items.topic: Antidiabetics: Diabetes in Pregnancy and Lactation
items.prompt: A pregnant woman at 26 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with gestational diabetes that is not controlled by diet alone. Which pharmacological statement is accurate regarding pregnancy and lactation?
options: Insulin does not normally cross the placenta and is the recommended therapy in pregnancy
Caloric restriction for weight loss combined with a GLP-1 agonist is first-line therapy
Insulin glargine is the preferred basal analogue specifically recommended during lactation
Sitagliptin and other DPP-4 inhibitors are first-line oral agents for gestational diabetes
items.rationale: Insulin does not normally cross the placenta and provides tight glycemic control to reduce the risk of congenital anomalies, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia. Weight reduction is not advised during pregnancy, DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists are not recommended, and insulin glargine should be avoided in breastfeeding women because it is unknown whether it is excreted in breast milk.

items.prompt: A 4-year-old child is newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. According to Diabetes Canada guidelines discussed in the text, what is the recommended HbA1C target for children younger than 6 years of age, and why is it more lenient?
options: Less than 8.0%, to minimize severe hypoglycemia linked to later cognitive impairment
Less than 6.5%, to prevent rapid autoimmune destruction of remaining beta-cells
Less than 7.5%, using twice-daily Humalog Mix25 as the standard pediatric regimen
Less than 7.0%, because young children have blunted counter-regulatory hormone release
items.rationale: Glycemic targets in children are graduated by age: < 8% for children younger than 6 years (to minimize severe hypoglycemia, which is linked to later cognitive impairment), <= 7.5% for children aged 6 to 12 years, and < 7% (adult target) for adolescents. Also note that Humalog Mix25 is not approved for children under 18 years.

items.topic: Antidiabetics: Glycemic Targets in Older Adults
items.prompt: According to Diabetes Canada guidelines, for which patient is a more lenient HbA1C target of 7.1% to 8.5% most appropriate instead of the standard < 7.0%?
options: An 84-year-old frail resident with dementia and recurrent severe hypoglycemia
A 35-year-old adult with new-onset type 2 diabetes managed on metformin therapy
A 28-year-old pregnant woman with pre-existing type 1 diabetes in her first trimester
A 50-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and a BMI of 29 kg/m²
items.rationale: Diabetes Canada recommends a more lenient HbA1C target (7.0%–8.5% or 7.1%–8.5%) for patients who are functionally dependent, have recurrent severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia unawareness, have limited life expectancy, or are frail older adults and/or living with dementia.

items.prompt: A patient with well-controlled type 2 diabetes is admitted with an acute asthma exacerbation and started on intravenous corticosteroids (methylprednisolone). How will corticosteroid therapy affect the patient's glycemic control?
options: It antagonizes the effects of insulin and increases plasma glucose concentrations
It potentiates oral antihyperglycemics and increases the risk of nocturnal hypoglycemia
It lowers the renal threshold for glucose and causes euglycemic ketoacidosis
It suppresses pancreatic alpha-cell glucagon secretion during fasting periods
items.rationale: Corticosteroids, thyroid hormones, niacin, diuretics (thiazides, furosemide), and sympathomimetics antagonize the hypoglycemic effects of insulin and oral antidiabetic drugs, resulting in elevated plasma glucose levels.

items.topic: Antidiabetics: DKA vs. Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
items.prompt: When comparing diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS), which clinical finding is characteristic of HHS rather than DKA?
options: Plasma glucose >= 34 mmol/L, osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg, and normal arterial pH
Rapid symptom onset under 2 days, arterial pH <= 7.3, and positive urine ketones
Presentation in patients under 65 years with serum bicarbonate <= 15 mmol/L
Moderate hyperglycemia (>= 14 mmol/L) with Kussmaul respirations and ketonemia
items.rationale: HHS typically develops over > 5 days in older adults (> 65 years) and features extreme hyperglycemia (>= 34 mmol/L), hyperosmolarity (> 320 mOsm/kg), severe dehydration, and normal arterial pH and bicarbonate without significant ketosis. DKA develops rapidly (< 2 days) with plasma glucose >= 14 mmol/L, positive ketones, pH <= 7.3, and HCO3 <= 15 mmol/L.

items.prompt: A 60-kg adult patient newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes is prescribed a starting total daily insulin dose of 0.4 units/kg/day subcutaneously, with 50% given as once-daily insulin glargine at bedtime. How many units of insulin glargine should the nurse administer at bedtime?
options: 24 units
12 units
15 units
30 units
items.rationale: Total daily insulin dose = 60 kg × 0.4 units/kg/day = 24 units/day. Since 50% of the total daily dose is ordered as bedtime insulin glargine, 24 units × 0.50 = 12 units.

items.prompt: Name the first-line oral biguanide medication for type 2 diabetes that must be held on the day of an iodinated contrast study and for at least 48 hours afterward to prevent lactic acidosis.
items.rationale: Metformin (Glucophage, Glumetza) is the only biguanide and is first-line oral therapy for type 2 diabetes. It must be held on the day of iodinated contrast studies and for at least 48 hours after to prevent contrast-induced nephropathy and lactic acidosis.

items.prompt: Name the pancreatic alpha-cell hormone administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly to treat severe hypoglycemia in an unconscious patient who lacks intravenous access.
items.rationale: Glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis to convert stored glycogen into glucose and is injected subcutaneously or intramuscularly when an unconscious hypoglycemic patient does not have IV access.

items.prompt: Which type of insulin is the ONLY insulin preparation that can be safely administered intravenously (e.g., for the management of diabetic ketoacidosis)?
items.rationale: Regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin ge Toronto) is a short-acting, clear unmodified solution and is the only insulin approved for intravenous bolus or infusion administration.

items.prompt: Name the alpha-glucosidase inhibitor that must be taken with the first bite of each main meal to delay intestinal carbohydrate absorption.
items.rationale: Acarbose (Glucobay) reversibly inhibits intestinal alpha-glucosidase and must be taken with the first bite of each main meal to blunt postprandial glucose elevations.

items.prompt: Which blood test (abbreviated A1C or HbA1C) measures the percentage of glycosylated hemoglobin to reflect average glycemic control over the preceding 2 to 3 months?
items.rationale: Hemoglobin A1C (HbA1C or A1C) measures the percentage of hemoglobin A irreversibly bound to glucose over the 90- to 120-day lifespan of red blood cells. The Diabetes Canada target for most adults with diabetes is < 7.0%.

items.prompt: What is the common 3-letter abbreviation for insulin isophane suspension, the cloudy intermediate-acting insulin that contains protamine and must be gently rolled before withdrawal?
items.rationale: NPH stands for neutral protamine Hagedorn (insulin isophane suspension), an opaque/cloudy intermediate-acting insulin with an onset of 2 to 4 hours, peak of 4 to 10 hours, and duration of 12 to 18 hours.

items.prompt: Name the long-acting basal insulin analogue (brand names Lantus, Basaglar, or Toujeo) that has an acidic pH of 4, forms subcutaneous microprecipitates, has no peak, and must never be mixed with other insulins.
items.rationale: Insulin glargine (Lantus, Basaglar, Toujeo) is a peakless long-acting basal insulin with a pH of 4 that precipitates in subcutaneous tissue for slow release over 20 to 24 hours (up to 30 hours for Toujeo).

items.prompt: Name the insulin-sensitizing thiazolidinedione (brand name Actos) that is contraindicated in NYHA Class III or IV heart failure due to fluid retention and edema.
items.rationale: Pioglitazone (Actos) is a thiazolidinedione (glitazone) that decreases insulin resistance but causes fluid retention, weight gain, and peripheral edema, making it contraindicated in NYHA Class III or IV heart failure.

items.prompt: Name the rapid-acting oral glinide (brand name GlucoNorm) taken 15 minutes before meals whose dose must be skipped whenever a meal is omitted.
items.rationale: Repaglinide (GlucoNorm) is a glinide (meglitinide) that stimulates rapid, short-duration insulin secretion from pancreatic beta-cells; patients take it 15 minutes before meals and skip the dose if a meal is missed.

items.prompt: Name the first Health Canada–approved oral DPP-4 inhibitor (brand name Januvia) dosed at 100 mg once daily that delays the breakdown of incretin hormones.
items.rationale: Sitagliptin phosphate monohydrate (Januvia) selectively inhibits dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4), increasing endogenous GLP-1 and GIP levels to improve glycemic control in type 2 diabetes.

items.title: New-Onset Type 1 Diabetes and Diabetic Ketoacidosis
items.scenario: Lucas, a 19-year-old university student (weight 65 kg), is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of severe polydipsia, polyuria, nausea, abdominal pain, and fruity-smelling breath. Vital signs: BP 98/62 mm Hg, HR 118 beats/min, RR 28 breaths/min (deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations), T 37.1°C. Lab results: plasma glucose 24.6 mmol/L, arterial pH 7.21, serum HCO3 12 mmol/L, serum potassium 3.8 mmol/L, serum sodium 134 mmol/L, and strongly positive serum and urine ketones.

question.prompt: Based on Lucas's presentation and laboratory values, which intravenous insulin order should the nurse anticipate after initiating IV fluid resuscitation?
options: Continuous intravenous infusion of regular insulin with hourly glucose monitoring
Intravenous bolus of insulin glargine 30 units every 6 hours with electrolyte checks
Continuous intravenous infusion of NPH insulin diluted in 0.9% sodium chloride
Subcutaneous injection of insulin lispro protamine suspension every 4 hours
question.rationale: Lucas presents with classic diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA: glucose >= 14 mmol/L, pH <= 7.3, HCO3 <= 15 mmol/L, positive ketones). Regular insulin is the only insulin that can be given intravenously and is administered as a continuous IV infusion with hourly glucose checks.

stages.update: After 3 hours of IV normal saline and a continuous regular insulin infusion, Lucas's plasma glucose decreases to 14.8 mmol/L. Repeat blood work shows his serum potassium has dropped from 3.8 mmol/L to 3.1 mmol/L.

question.prompt: Why did Lucas's serum potassium level drop to 3.1 mmol/L during the regular insulin infusion, and what is the nurse's priority action?
options: Insulin shifts potassium into cells; contact the prescriber for IV potassium replacement
Insulin increases renal potassium excretion; administer an oral loop diuretic as ordered
Acidosis traps potassium in the liver; pause the IV fluids and give subcutaneous glucagon
Saline infusion dilutes intracellular potassium; increase the regular insulin infusion rate
question.rationale: Insulin promotes the intracellular shift of potassium and magnesium into cells along with glucose, rapidly lowering serum potassium levels (normal range 3.5–5.0 mmol/L). Potassium replacement is essential in DKA management to prevent life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmias.

stages.update: By hospital day 2, Lucas's DKA has resolved. He is alert, tolerating a regular diabetic diet, and transitioning to a subcutaneous basal-bolus regimen consisting of insulin glargine (Lantus) at bedtime and insulin lispro (Humalog) before meals. His 0745 capillary blood glucose is 8.6 mmol/L, and his breakfast tray is on the unit.

question.prompt: When should the nurse administer Lucas's pre-breakfast dose of subcutaneous insulin lispro (Humalog)?
options: Within 15 minutes before he begins eating his breakfast
Thirty to 45 minutes before the breakfast tray arrives
Sixty minutes prior to the scheduled morning mealtime
Mixed in the same syringe with his insulin glargine dose
question.rationale: Insulin lispro is a rapid-acting insulin analogue with an onset of 10 to 15 minutes. It must be given within 15 minutes before a meal, only after verifying that the meal tray has arrived and the patient is ready to eat.

stages.update: That afternoon at 1400, after walking around the hospital unit for 30 minutes without eating all of his lunch, Lucas tells the nurse he feels shaky, anxious, and sweaty. A bedside capillary blood glucose check reads 3.3 mmol/L.

question.prompt: Lucas is awake and able to swallow safely. Which sequence of actions should the nurse implement?
options: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, retest in 15 minutes, and follow with a protein snack
Administer 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV push and withhold all basal and bolus insulin for 24 hours
Provide 2 tablespoons of peanut butter with milk and recheck capillary glucose in 60 minutes
Inject 1 mg of glucagon intramuscularly, turn him on his side, and keep him NPO until supper
question.rationale: For mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia (< 4 mmol/L) in a conscious patient, Diabetes Canada guidelines specify giving 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, retesting plasma glucose in 15 minutes (retreating with 15 g if still < 4 mmol/L), and following with a meal or a 15 g carbohydrate plus protein snack if the next meal is more than 1 hour away.

items.title: Metformin Management and Contrast Imaging in Type 2 Diabetes
items.scenario: Margaret, a 61-year-old woman with obesity (BMI 33 kg/m²), hypertension, and dyslipidemia, was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 4 months ago. Despite 3 months of dietary modifications and aerobic exercise, her HbA1C is 7.9% and her fasting plasma glucose is 8.8 mmol/L. Her eGFR is 78 mL/min, and she has no history of heart or liver disease.

question.prompt: According to Diabetes Canada clinical practice guidelines, which oral medication is recommended as first-line pharmacotherapy for Margaret, and what is a key advantage of this drug for her?
options: Metformin (Glucophage), which improves insulin sensitivity without causing weight gain
Pioglitazone (Actos), which acts rapidly before meals and promotes osmotic fluid loss
Glyburide (Diabeta), which preserves beta-cells by suppressing endogenous insulin output
Acarbose (Glucobay), which directly inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis during overnight fasts
question.rationale: Metformin is the first-line oral antihyperglycemic recommended by Diabetes Canada for type 2 diabetes, especially in patients with a BMI over 25. Unlike sulfonylureas or glitazones, it does not stimulate insulin secretion, does not cause weight gain (may cause modest weight loss), and rarely causes hypoglycemia as monotherapy.

stages.update: Margaret starts metformin 500 mg PO twice daily. One week later, she calls the clinic stating she is experiencing mild nausea, abdominal bloating, and loose stools and wants to stop taking the pills.

question.prompt: What is the nurse's most appropriate response to help Margaret manage these adverse effects?
options: Advise her to take metformin with meals, as early gastrointestinal effects usually subside
Instruct her to take the tablets on an empty stomach 1 hour before meals to speed absorption
Tell her to stop metformin and request a switch to a sulfonylurea due to drug intolerance
Recommend taking a salicylate with each dose to reduce intestinal cramping and bloating
question.rationale: GI adverse effects (bloating, nausea, cramping, fullness, diarrhea) are common when starting metformin. They are usually self-limiting and can be minimized by taking the medication with food and titrating the dose slowly.

stages.update: Eight months later, Margaret presents to the hospital with acute right upper quadrant pain and is scheduled for an abdominal CT scan with intravenous iodinated contrast media this afternoon.

question.prompt: What action must the nurse take regarding Margaret's metformin therapy in relation to the contrast-enhanced CT scan?
options: Hold metformin the day of the scan and for at least 48 hours until renal function is verified
Give the morning metformin dose with 500 mL of water 1 hour prior to contrast administration
Hold metformin for 4 hours before the scan and resume therapy once post-scan voiding is noted
Substitute canagliflozin on the morning of the scan to promote renal excretion of contrast dye
question.rationale: Iodinated radiocontrast media can cause acute kidney injury (contrast-induced nephropathy), leading to metformin accumulation and potentially fatal lactic acidosis. Metformin must be discontinued the day of the test and for at least 48 hours afterward, and restarted only after confirming normal renal function.

stages.update: One year later, Margaret's HbA1C rises to 8.2% on maximal metformin therapy, and her prescriber adds modified-release gliclazide (Diamicron MR) 30 mg once daily with breakfast. She also takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension.

question.prompt: When reviewing Margaret's medication list, how does hydrochlorothiazide (a thiazide diuretic) interact with gliclazide?
options: It increases gliclazide metabolism and antagonizes its glucose-lowering effectiveness
It inhibits hepatic clearance of gliclazide and precipitates severe hypoglycemia
It delays intestinal absorption of gliclazide unless doses are separated by 4 hours
It displaces gliclazide from plasma proteins and increases the risk of lactic acidosis
question.rationale: According to Table 33.5, diuretics (thiazides and furosemide), corticosteroids, and oral contraceptives increase the metabolism and antagonize the effects of gliclazide and insulin, resulting in decreased glucose-lowering effectiveness and elevated plasma glucose levels.

items.title: Cardiorenal Comorbidities and Second-Line Oral Agents
items.scenario: Robert, a 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and NYHA Class III heart failure (left ventricular ejection fraction 30%), is seen in the outpatient clinic. He currently takes metformin 500 mg twice daily, ramipril, carvedilol, and digoxin. His HbA1C is 8.4%, BP is 136/82 mm Hg, and eGFR is 64 mL/min.

question.prompt: A medical resident suggests adding pioglitazone (Actos) to Robert's regimen. Why should the nurse question this prescription?
options: Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and edema and is contraindicated in Class III heart failure
Pioglitazone induces osmotic diuresis and severe volume depletion in patients taking ramipril
Pioglitazone blocks beta-adrenergic receptors and worsens bradycardia when combined with carvedilol
Pioglitazone inhibits renal tubular digoxin secretion and causes life-threatening hypokalemia
question.rationale: Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) cause fluid retention, edema, and weight gain that can precipitate or worsen heart failure. They are contraindicated in NYHA Class III or IV heart failure.

stages.update: Instead of pioglitazone, the prescriber orders canagliflozin (Invokana) 100 mg PO once daily before breakfast as add-on therapy for Robert's type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease.

question.prompt: Because Robert is taking digoxin concurrently with canagliflozin, which specific drug interaction must the nurse monitor for?
options: Canagliflozin can increase serum digoxin concentrations, requiring monitoring for digoxin toxicity
Canagliflozin accelerates hepatic digoxin clearance, increasing the risk of rapid atrial fibrillation
Digoxin competes with canagliflozin at proximal renal tubules, blunting urinary glucose excretion
Canagliflozin chelates oral digoxin in the small intestine, reducing digoxin bioavailability by half
question.rationale: Canagliflozin increases serum digoxin concentrations, so patients taking digoxin must have their digoxin levels and clinical signs of toxicity monitored closely.

stages.update: At his 4-week follow-up visit, Robert reports that he feels dizzy and light-headed whenever he stands up quickly in the morning, and he notices he is urinating much more frequently.

question.prompt: What is the physiological cause of Robert's orthostatic dizziness while taking canagliflozin?
options: Increased urinary glucose excretion causes osmotic diuresis and intravascular volume depletion
Direct alpha-adrenergic blockade in peripheral arterioles causes systemic arterial vasodilation
Excessive pancreatic insulin secretion triggers early morning neuroglycopenic light-headedness
Sodium retention in the distal renal tubules shifts fluid into the interstitial tissue spaces
question.rationale: SGLT-2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption, causing glucosuria and osmotic diuresis. This can result in intravascular volume depletion, dehydration, hypotension, orthostatic dizziness, and syncope.

stages.update: Three months later, Robert develops a severe viral gastroenteritis with vomiting and poor oral intake. He presents to urgent care with nausea, abdominal pain, tachypnea, and confusion. His plasma glucose is only 11.8 mmol/L, but his blood pH is 7.24, HCO3 is 14 mmol/L, and serum ketones are strongly positive.

question.prompt: Which SGLT-2 inhibitor–related complication is Robert experiencing?
options: SGLT-2 inhibitor–associated diabetic ketoacidosis with mildly elevated blood glucose
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state secondary to severe viral gastrointestinal fluid loss
Metformin-induced lactic acidosis precipitated by concurrent digoxin and ramipril use
Somogyi rebound hyperglycemia triggered by nocturnal counter-regulatory hormone surges
question.rationale: As highlighted in the Health Canada safety review, SGLT-2 inhibitors (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin) can precipitate diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) unexpectedly in patients with type 2 diabetes, often with only mildly or moderately elevated plasma glucose levels.

items.title: Postprandial Hyperglycemia, Incretin Therapy, and Pancreatitis
items.topic: Antidiabetics: Alpha-Glucosidase Inhibitors, Glinides & Incretin Therapy
items.scenario: Amira, a 54-year-old nurse who works rotating shifts and frequently has delayed or missed meals at work, has type 2 diabetes. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, along with acarbose (Glucobay) 50 mg three times daily and repaglinide (GlucoNorm) 1 mg before meals.

question.prompt: Today during a busy shift, Amira is unable to eat lunch. How should she manage her midday doses of repaglinide and acarbose?
options: Skip both the midday repaglinide and acarbose doses since she is omitting lunch
Take the midday repaglinide to prevent stress hyperglycemia and hold the acarbose
Hold the midday repaglinide to avoid hypoglycemia and take the acarbose as scheduled
Combine the missed midday doses with her evening doses before eating supper at 1800
question.rationale: Repaglinide (a glinide) stimulates insulin release and must be skipped whenever a meal is omitted to prevent hypoglycemia. Acarbose (an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor) works locally in the small intestine to delay carbohydrate digestion and must be taken with the first bite of a meal, so it is also omitted if no meal is eaten.

stages.update: The next day, Amira takes her repaglinide and acarbose with the first bite of breakfast, but is called away to an emergency after eating only two bites. Forty-five minutes later, she feels shaky, weak, and diaphoretic, and her blood glucose is 3.0 mmol/L.

question.prompt: Because Amira takes acarbose (which blocks the intestinal breakdown of sucrose/disaccharides), what specific simple sugar (monosaccharide) in tablet form must she use to rapidly reverse her hypoglycemia?
question.rationale: Acarbose inhibits alpha-glucosidase in the small intestine, preventing the hydrolysis of sucrose (table sugar) and complex carbohydrates. Patients taking acarbose must treat hypoglycemia with pure glucose (dextrose) tablets (or honey/milk if tablets are unavailable).

stages.update: Because of intolerable flatulence and diarrhea from acarbose, Amira's prescriber discontinues acarbose and repaglinide and initiates subcutaneous liraglutide (Victoza) 0.6 mg once daily.

question.prompt: What should the nurse teach Amira about how liraglutide (an incretin mimetic / GLP-1 receptor agonist) helps manage her type 2 diabetes and weight?
options: It enhances glucose-dependent insulin release, lowers glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and increases satiety
It blocks proximal renal tubular glucose reabsorption, promotes glucosuria, and reduces systolic blood pressure
It activates nuclear peroxisome receptors, increases adipocyte glucose uptake, and reduces hepatic lipid output
It inhibits intestinal disaccharidase enzymes, delays complex carbohydrate digestion, and blunts glucose spikes
question.rationale: Liraglutide (Victoza) is a GLP-1 receptor agonist (incretin mimetic) that stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion, reduces postprandial glucagon production, slows gastric emptying, and increases satiety, typically resulting in weight loss.

stages.update: Six weeks after her liraglutide dose is titrated up to 1.2 mg daily, Amira develops acute, severe, boring epigastric pain that radiates straight through to her back, accompanied by persistent nausea and vomiting.

question.prompt: Which rare but life-threatening adverse effect of incretin mimetics (and DPP-4 inhibitors) should the nurse suspect?
options: Acute hemorrhagic or necrotizing pancreatitis
Contrast-induced nephropathy and renal failure
Cholestatic jaundice and hepatic cirrhosis
Mesenteric venous thrombosis and bowel ileus
question.rationale: Both incretin mimetics (exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, albiglutide) and DPP-4 inhibitors have been associated with postmarketing cases of acute, hemorrhagic, or necrotizing pancreatitis after initiation and dose increases. The drug must be stopped immediately and the patient evaluated.

items.title: Perioperative NPO Management and Mixed Insulins
items.topic: Antidiabetics: NPH/Regular Insulin Mixing, NPO Status & Sick-Day Care
items.scenario: Walter, a 64-year-old retired carpenter with type 2 diabetes, takes subcutaneous NPH insulin (Humulin N) 22 units and regular insulin (Humulin R) 8 units every morning before breakfast, and NPH 14 units and regular 6 units before supper. He is admitted to the surgical unit for an elective knee arthroplasty scheduled for 0900 today and has been NPO since midnight.

question.prompt: At 0700 on the morning of surgery, Walter remains NPO and is receiving an IV infusion of Ringer's lactate. His capillary blood glucose is 6.4 mmol/L. There are no specific NPO insulin parameters written on the chart. What is the nurse's priority action?
options: Withhold the morning NPH and regular insulin and contact the prescriber to clarify NPO orders
Administer the full scheduled doses of NPH and regular insulin to prevent surgical stress hyperglycemia
Administer the 22 units of NPH insulin for basal coverage and hold the 8 units of regular insulin
Add the scheduled regular insulin dose to the Ringer's lactate bag to infuse over the next 8 hours
question.rationale: When a patient is placed on NPO status for surgery or diagnostic procedures, administering usual mealtime or intermediate-acting insulin without caloric intake carries a high risk of severe hypoglycemia. If specific NPO orders are not written, the nurse must hold the dose and contact the health care provider for instructions.

stages.update: Postoperatively on day 1, Walter is placed on intravenous methylprednisolone for severe joint inflammation and is resuming his normal diabetic diet. His pre-breakfast blood glucose has risen to 13.8 mmol/L, compared with his usual home readings of 5.8 to 6.5 mmol/L. Walter asks, "I barely ate anything yesterday! Why is my blood sugar so high?"

question.prompt: What is the nurse's best explanation for Walter's elevated plasma glucose levels?
options: Surgical stress hormones and corticosteroid therapy both antagonize insulin and raise blood glucose
Preoperative fasting depletes hepatic glycogen stores and impairs peripheral insulin receptor binding
General anesthetic agents suppress pancreatic beta-cell insulin synthesis for 48 hours after surgery
Intravenous Ringer's lactate solution is converted into glucose by the kidneys during recovery
question.rationale: Physical stress (surgery, infection, trauma) triggers release of counter-regulatory hormones (cortisol, epinephrine) that mobilize glucagon and hepatic glucose, while exogenous corticosteroids directly antagonize the hypoglycemic effects of insulin, causing significant hyperglycemia.

stages.update: Before breakfast on postoperative day 2, the nurse prepares to administer Walter's scheduled 22 units of NPH insulin (cloudy) and 8 units of regular insulin (clear) mixed in one U-100 insulin syringe, along with a newly ordered 4-unit correction dose of regular insulin (total 12 units regular + 22 units NPH = 34 units total).

question.prompt: Which preparation and administration technique must the nurse follow for this mixed insulin dose?
options: Gently roll the NPH vial, verify the dose with a second RN, draw up regular before NPH, and inject within 5 minutes
Gently roll the NPH vial, verify the dose with a second RN, draw up NPH before regular, and inject within 5 minutes
Shake the NPH vial to suspend crystals, draw up regular before NPH in a U-100 syringe, and wait 15 minutes to inject
Gently roll the NPH vial, draw up regular and NPH in separate tuberculin syringes, and inject within 2 cm of the navel
question.rationale: Insulin is a high-alert medication requiring an independent double-check with another RN. The cloudy NPH vial is gently rolled (never shaken), clear regular insulin is drawn up before cloudy NPH ('clear before cloudy'), only a U-100 insulin syringe with a preattached needle is used, and freshly mixed regular/NPH insulin must be injected within 5 minutes of mixing to prevent binding and altered activity.

stages.update: Walter is preparing for discharge home on his regular and NPH insulin regimen. He asks the nurse what he should do if he catches the flu at home and feels too nauseated to eat his normal meals.

question.prompt: Which sick-day management instruction should the nurse provide to Walter?
options: "Continue taking your insulin, monitor blood glucose closely, and contact your prescriber for sick-day guidance."
"Withhold your NPH and regular insulin injections while febrile until you can tolerate three full meals daily."
"Take half of your morning NPH insulin dose and defer blood glucose testing until your nausea resolves with meals."
"Double your regular insulin dose every 4 hours during a fever and restrict oral fluids to prevent vomiting."
question.rationale: Acute illness and fever trigger counter-regulatory stress hormones that elevate plasma glucose levels even when food intake is reduced. Patients should be taught never to stop taking their insulin during illness, to monitor blood glucose frequently, maintain hydration/carbohydrate intake as advised, and contact their health care provider for specific sick-day instructions.

items.prompt: A 64-year-old patient with a history of transient ischemic attacks and a healed duodenal ulcer is prescribed daily acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) for thromboprevention. Which daily dosage is most appropriate to achieve platelet inhibition while minimizing gastrointestinal bleeding risk?
options: 3.6 g orally in divided daily doses
650 mg orally twice daily with food
325 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours
81 mg orally once daily with meals
items.rationale: An 81-mg daily dose of ASA effectively and irreversibly inhibits platelet thromboxane A2 synthesis and is preferred over 325 mg for patients with an elevated risk of bleeding, such as a history of peptic ulcer disease or stroke. Higher doses (325–650 mg q4h or 3.6–5.4 g/day) are used for pain, fever, or rheumatic inflammation and carry a much higher risk of GI ulceration.

items.prompt: A patient arrives at the emergency department with suspected acute coronary syndrome. The prescriber orders acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) 325 mg PO stat. Which administration instruction should the nurse give the patient to achieve a peak plasma concentration in approximately 20 minutes?
options: Swallow a non–enteric-coated tablet whole with water
Dissolve an enteric-coated tablet in warm fruit juice
Chew a non–enteric-coated tablet before swallowing
Chew an enteric-coated tablet with a glass of milk
items.rationale: In the setting of an acute coronary syndrome, chewing a non–enteric-coated ASA tablet produces a peak plasma concentration in about 20 minutes. Chewing enteric-coated tablets still results in a delayed peak of approximately 2 hours, and enteric-coated or sustained-release preparations are normally not meant to be chewed.

items.prompt: Why does a single antiplatelet dose of acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) prolong bleeding tendencies for approximately 10 days, even though its plasma elimination half-life is 3 to 6 hours?
options: ASA stimulates prostacyclin synthetase in vascular endothelium for two weeks
ASA accumulates in bone marrow megakaryocytes and releases over 10 days
ASA suppresses hepatic synthesis of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors
ASA irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) within circulating platelets
items.rationale: Unlike other NSAIDs, ASA is an irreversible inhibitor of COX-1 receptors within platelets, preventing the formation of thromboxane A2. Because platelets lack a nucleus and cannot synthesize new COX-1 enzyme, the antiplatelet effect persists for the lifespan of the platelet (approximately 10 days).

items.prompt: A nurse is conducting a pre-administration assessment for a patient who has been prescribed acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) for osteoarthritis. Which cluster of conditions in the patient's history represents the 'aspirin triad' that places the patient at high risk for a severe hypersensitivity reaction?
options: Hypertension, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease
Bronchial asthma, nasal polyps, and chronic rhinitis
Atopic eczema, allergic conjunctivitis, and urticaria
Peptic ulcer disease, chronic tinnitus, and gouty arthritis
items.rationale: The 'aspirin triad' consists of asthma, nasal polyps, and rhinitis. Patients with this triad or a history of asthma and wheezing have a significantly increased incidence of severe allergic bronchospasm and hypersensitivity reactions to aspirin.

items.prompt: A parent calls the telehealth line stating that their 8-year-old child has influenza B with a temperature of 39.1°C and asks about giving the child an over-the-counter cold preparation containing salicylate. Which response by the nurse is priority?
options: Avoid giving any salicylate product due to the risk of Reye's syndrome
Give half the adult salicylate dose with milk to reduce gastric distress
Switch to an enteric-coated salicylate tablet to protect hepatic function
Administer the salicylate product unless vesicular chicken pox lesions appear
items.rationale: Aspirin and any OTC preparations containing salicylates are contraindicated in children and adolescents with viral illnesses (such as influenza or chicken pox) due to the risk of Reye's syndrome, an acute, potentially fatal illness characterized by encephalopathy and fatty liver degeneration. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen should be used instead.

items.prompt: A 72-year-old patient who has been taking high doses of acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) for rheumatoid arthritis reports a constant ringing in both ears and muffled hearing. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: An idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction requiring subcutaneous epinephrine
A classic manifestation of chronic salicylate intoxication (salicylism)
An expected transient effect of prostaglandin inhibition that resolves
An early indicator of cerebrovascular ischemia from COX-2 inhibition
items.rationale: Tinnitus and hearing loss are the most common manifestations of chronic salicylate intoxication (salicylism) in adults. The prescriber should be notified so that the medication can be discontinued or the dosage reduced.

items.prompt: A patient is brought to the emergency department 7 hours after ingesting a large bottle of acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) tablets in an acute overdose. For which clinical finding would the health care team anticipate initiating hemodialysis?
options: Transient elevation of serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels
Unresponsive metabolic acidosis with an arterial blood pH of 7.05
An estimated ingested salicylate dose of 150 mg/kg of body weight
Moderate tinnitus accompanied by epigastric discomfort and nausea
items.rationale: In severe acute salicylate intoxication, hemodialysis is indicated for high serum salicylate levels, unresponsive acidosis (pH less than 7.1), impaired kidney function or kidney failure, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, persistent CNS symptoms (seizures, coma), or progressive clinical deterioration.

items.prompt: While inspecting a patient's home medications during a community health visit, the nurse notices a strong vinegar-like odour coming from the patient's bottle of acetylsalicylic acid (ASA). What instruction should the nurse provide?
options: Take the remaining tablets with an antacid to neutralize excess acid
Leave the bottle open in a dry room to allow acetic acid vapours to clear
Dissolve the tablets in a full glass of water prior to administration
Discard the tablets and purchase a fresh bottle due to drug breakdown
items.rationale: A vinegary odour coming from aspirin tablets is a sign of chemical breakdown (hydrolysis into salicylic and acetic acids). The medication should be discarded and replaced.

items.prompt: When comparing nonselective NSAIDs with selective cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitors, which statement accurately describes the physiological role of the COX-1 enzyme isoform?
options: COX-1 synthesizes prostaglandins that protect gastric mucosa and aid platelet aggregation
COX-1 constricts the afferent renal arteriole to reduce renal blood flow in dehydration
COX-1 is induced at sites of tissue injury to generate inflammatory pain and fever
COX-1 converts arachidonic acid into leukotrienes that mediate airway bronchospasm
items.rationale: COX-1 is the constitutive isoform that synthesizes prostaglandins with beneficial housekeeping functions, such as maintaining an intact gastrointestinal mucosa and producing thromboxane A2 in platelets. Blocking COX-1 with nonselective NSAIDs accounts for their ulcerogenic and bleeding adverse effects.

items.prompt: A patient with bone cancer pain is prescribed an NSAID in addition to a scheduled opioid analgesic. The patient asks why an over-the-counter class of pain reliever is being added to a strong opioid. What is the nurse's best explanation?
options: The NSAID removes the analgesic ceiling of the opioid so lower frequencies are needed
Combining both drugs targets pain via two mechanisms and provides an opioid-sparing effect
NSAIDs prevent opioid-induced respiratory depression by acting on the preoptic hypothalamus
Adding an NSAID slows hepatic opioid conjugation and prolongs central receptor binding
items.rationale: NSAIDs inhibit peripheral prostaglandin synthesis while opioids act centrally on opioid receptors. Combining them attacks pain by two different mechanisms and produces an opioid-sparing effect, allowing lower doses of the opioid to be used with fewer opioid adverse effects.

items.prompt: A patient taking maximum recommended doses of ibuprofen for lumbar strain tells the nurse, 'If 400 mg helps a little, taking 1 200 mg at once should knock the pain out.' Which pharmacological principle should guide the nurse's teaching?
options: NSAIDs undergo saturable first-pass hepatic inactivation when single doses exceed 600 mg
NSAIDs exhibit a ceiling effect where higher doses increase toxicity without added analgesia
High single doses of ibuprofen activate lipoxygenase pathways and worsen joint inflammation
Ibuprofen requires metabolic activation by xanthine oxidase, which saturates above 400 mg
items.rationale: Unlike opioids, NSAIDs demonstrate a ceiling effect: increasing the dosage beyond recommended maximums does not produce greater analgesic effect but significantly increases the risk of serious gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiovascular adverse effects.

items.prompt: A 68-year-old patient is scheduled for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery tomorrow. Which medication order on the postoperative pain management protocol must the nurse question?
options: Docusate sodium 100 mg PO twice daily while receiving opioid analgesics
Morphine sulphate 2 mg IV every 2 hours PRN for breakthrough chest pain
Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN for mild pain or low-grade fever
Ketorolac tromethamine 15 mg IV every 6 hours PRN for postoperative pain
items.rationale: Per Health Canada warnings required on all NSAID packaging, NSAIDs (such as ketorolac) are strictly contraindicated for the treatment of perioperative pain in the setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery due to the heightened risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, MI, and stroke.

items.prompt: A pregnant patient at 34 weeks' gestation asks the nurse if she can take naproxen for her lower back ache. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
options: Take naproxen at bedtime with food to minimize morning nausea and blood pressure spikes
Use naproxen intermittently during the third trimester with a full glass of milk or water
Avoid NSAIDs after 32 weeks' gestation due to bleeding and fetal ductal closure risks
Switch to regular-strength aspirin after 32 weeks' gestation to avoid placental transfer
items.rationale: Pregnant women should avoid using NSAIDs after 32 weeks' gestation due to the risk of antiplatelet/prolonged bleeding effects, prenatal constriction or closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus, and neonatal NSAID toxicity.

items.prompt: Although NSAIDs are avoided in late pregnancy, a neonate born prematurely is diagnosed with a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Which medications from this chapter may be administered to the newborn to promote closure of the ductus arteriosus?
options: Ibuprofen or indomethacin
Allopurinol or colchicine
Acetylsalicylic acid or probenecid
Celecoxib or meloxicam
items.rationale: Because prostaglandins maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus, inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis with intravenous ibuprofen or indomethacin (Indocid P.D.A.) is used therapeutically in newborns to close a patent ductus arteriosus.

items.prompt: A 76-year-old patient taking ramipril (an ACE inhibitor) and furosemide for hypertension and heart failure begins taking over-the-counter ibuprofen daily for knee osteoarthritis. Why does this combination place the patient at high risk for acute kidney injury?
options: Afferent arteriole constriction from the NSAID and efferent dilation from the ACE inhibitor lower GFR
Ibuprofen forms insoluble chelate crystals with ramipril in the renal tubules and obstructs urine flow
NSAIDs stimulate adrenal aldosterone release and precipitate acute hypokalemic nephropathy with diuretics
ACE inhibitors block hepatic glucuronidation of ibuprofen and cause direct proximal tubular cell necrosis
items.rationale: NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandins, resulting in vasoconstriction of the afferent renal arteriole, while ACE inhibitors and ARBs cause vasodilation of the efferent arteriole. Together (especially with diuretics or dehydration), they cause a drastic reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and can precipitate acute kidney injury. In addition, NSAIDs reduce the hypotensive and diuretic effects of ACE inhibitors and diuretics.

items.prompt: A 58-year-old patient with uncontrolled hypertension and a history of angina asks the nurse about renewing a prescription for diclofenac sodium (Voltaren) 75 mg twice daily for hip osteoarthritis. Which Health Canada safety update is most relevant to this patient's care?
options: Diclofenac at doses of 150 mg/day or higher increases cardiovascular risk in patients with heart disease
Diclofenac is contraindicated in adults over 55 years of age due to the risk of acute hepatic necrosis
Diclofenac precipitates optic neuritis and retinopathy when combined with antihypertensive medications
Diclofenac therapy must be limited to 7 days because prolonged administration induces bone marrow aplasia
items.rationale: In 2014, Health Canada updated its warning on diclofenac to highlight an increased risk of cardiovascular events (MI, stroke), particularly at higher doses (150 mg/day or more) and with longer duration of use. Patients with a history of or risk factors for heart disease, stroke, or uncontrolled hypertension are at greater risk.

items.prompt: A 42-year-old patient is receiving ketorolac tromethamine (Toradol) 30 mg IM every 6 hours following open reduction and internal fixation of an ankle fracture. What is the maximum permitted duration of ketorolac therapy for a postsurgical patient?
options: Up to 10 days
Up to 14 days
Up to 7 days
Up to 5 days
items.rationale: Because of the high potential for severe renal and gastrointestinal adverse effects, ketorolac use must not exceed 5 days in postsurgical patients (and up to 7 days for patients with acute musculoskeletal pain).

items.prompt: A 70-year-old patient is prescribed intramuscular ketorolac tromethamine for acute severe flank pain. According to standard dosage guidelines, what is the maximum total daily intramuscular dose of ketorolac for an adult older than 65 years?
options: Maximum of 120 mg/day
Maximum of 40 mg/day
Maximum of 90 mg/day
Maximum of 60 mg/day
items.rationale: For intramuscular ketorolac tromethamine, the maximum daily dosage is 120 mg/day for adults under 65 years of age, but it is reduced to a maximum of 60 mg/day for adults older than 65 years (and maximum 40 mg/day for the oral route).

items.prompt: A nurse is preparing to administer ketorolac tromethamine (Toradol) 15 mg IM to an adult patient with acute orthopedic pain. Which administration technique is correct?
options: Inject rapidly into the anterior deltoid or abdominal subcutaneous tissue
Administer on an empty stomach at least 2 hours before scheduled meals
Administer the injection slowly and deeply into a large muscle mass
Mix the ketorolac in one syringe with morphine to reduce site discomfort
items.rationale: Intramuscular ketorolac should be administered slowly and deeply into a large muscle mass to minimize local tissue irritation and pain.

items.prompt: A 13-year-old patient is admitted with a painful tibial fracture. The resident physician mentions ordering ketorolac (Toradol) for pain relief. What should the nurse communicate to the prescriber?
options: Ketorolac is approved for children over 12 years when dosed at 0.5 mg/kg
Ketorolac is not recommended in children under 16 due to unestablished safety
Ketorolac must be administered via rectal suppository in pediatric patients
Ketorolac is contraindicated in adolescents because it triggers Reye's syndrome
items.rationale: Ketorolac is not recommended for use in children under age 16, as safety and efficacy in children have not been established. Ibuprofen or acetaminophen (or opioids for severe pain) are used instead.

items.prompt: A patient newly started on ibuprofen 400 mg PO every 6 hours for rheumatoid arthritis calls the clinic after 2 days stating, 'The pills take the edge off my pain for a few hours, but my knuckles are still just as swollen in the morning.' What is the nurse's best response?
options: Advise stopping ibuprofen since persistent swelling at 48 hours indicates treatment failure
Explain that analgesia begins in 30 to 60 minutes, but anti-inflammatory effects take 7 days
Instruct the patient to increase the dose to 800 mg every 4 hours until joint swelling subsides
Suggest adding enteric-coated aspirin 325 mg twice daily for synergistic anti-inflammatory action
items.rationale: Oral ibuprofen has an analgesic onset of 30 to 60 minutes, but its full therapeutic anti-inflammatory action takes approximately 7 days (1 week or longer). Combining aspirin with another NSAID is contraindicated because it reduces NSAID absorption and increases GI toxicity with no therapeutic advantage.

items.prompt: According to Health Canada safety warnings, at what daily dosage threshold does prescription-strength ibuprofen pose a significantly increased risk of serious cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke?
options: 800 mg/day or higher
1 200 mg/day or higher
2 400 mg/day or more
1 600 mg/day or higher
items.rationale: Health Canada issued a safety warning regarding the increased risk of serious cardiovascular events (stroke, MI) associated with high doses of ibuprofen of at least 2 400 mg/day. The risk increases with dose size and duration of use.

items.prompt: A patient with hypertension controlled with lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) requires a propionic acid derivative for osteoarthritis. Why might the prescriber select naproxen rather than ibuprofen for this patient?
options: Naproxen is less likely than ibuprofen to blunt the hypotensive effects of ACE inhibitors
Naproxen selectively inhibits central COX-2 enzymes while sparing renal prostaglandins
Naproxen acts as a direct arterial vasodilator that enhances ACE inhibitor efficacy
Naproxen undergoes biliary elimination and avoids glomerular filtration competition
items.rationale: Naproxen is the second most commonly used NSAID and is reported to have a somewhat better adverse effect profile and fewer drug interactions with ACE inhibitors than ibuprofen, which is more likely to hinder the desired hypotensive effects of ACE inhibitors.

items.prompt: An 18-month-old child weighing 12 kg is prescribed oral ibuprofen suspension 10 mg/kg/dose every 6 hours PRN for fever. How many milligrams should the nurse administer per dose, and is this within the safe pediatric dosage range?
options: 120 mg per dose; yes, it is within the 5 to 10 mg/kg/dose safe range
60 mg per dose; yes, because the maximum pediatric dose is 5 mg/kg/dose
240 mg per dose; yes, because young children clear ibuprofen rapidly
120 mg per dose; no, it exceeds the maximum pediatric single dose of 80 mg
items.rationale: For infants and children, the recommended ibuprofen dosage is 5 to 10 mg/kg/dose every 6 to 8 hours (up to a maximum of 40 mg/kg/day or 400 mg/dose). For a 12-kg child, 10 mg/kg equals 120 mg per dose (and up to 480 mg/day if given 4 times, corresponding to 40 mg/kg/day).

items.prompt: A nurse is reviewing the allergy history of a patient newly prescribed celecoxib (Celebrex) 200 mg PO daily for ankylosing spondylitis. An allergy to which medication class is a specific contraindication to administering celecoxib?
options: Macrolide antibiotics
Calcium channel blockers
Sulfonamide antimicrobials
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics
items.rationale: Celecoxib contains a sulfonamide moiety and is contraindicated in patients with a known sulfa (sulfonamide) allergy, in addition to patients with an allergy to aspirin or other NSAIDs.

items.prompt: A patient prescribed celecoxib (Celebrex) asks the nurse why two other drugs in the same family—rofecoxib (Vioxx) and valdecoxib (Bextra)—were taken off the Canadian market. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Clinical data linked them to an increased risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, and death
Postmarketing studies showed higher rates of gastric perforation than nonselective aspirin
Surveillance data revealed a high incidence of aplastic anemia and severe agranulocytosis
Clinical trials demonstrated severe hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis in older adult patients
items.rationale: Rofecoxib (Vioxx) and valdecoxib (Bextra) were withdrawn from the Canadian market after their use was linked to an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and death. Celecoxib is the only COX-2 inhibitor remaining on the market and also carries cardiovascular risk warnings.

items.prompt: When teaching a patient about medication safety with celecoxib (Celebrex), the nurse warns the patient to check the pharmacy label carefully at each refill because Celebrex is a high-alert 'look-alike, sound-alike' drug commonly confused with which medications?
options: Celestone (betamethasone) and CellCept (mycophenolate)
Cilazapril (Inhibace) and Ciprofloxacin (Cipro)
Cephalexin (Keflex) and Cetirizine (Reactine)
Celexa (citalopram) and Cerebyx (fosphenytoin)
items.rationale: Patient and nursing safety teaching specifically highlights that Celebrex (celecoxib) has a look-alike, sound-alike name that may be confused with the antidepressant Celexa (citalopram) or the anticonvulsant Cerebyx (fosphenytoin).

items.prompt: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis who experienced epigastric distress with piroxicam is switched to nabumetone, another enolic acid derivative. Why is nabumetone generally better tolerated by the gastrointestinal tract than other enolic acid derivatives?
options: It acts as a selective leukotriene antagonist without inhibiting cyclooxygenase
It forms a protective sucralfate-like aluminum complex over gastric erosions
It has a relatively nonacidic chemical structure compared with other NSAIDs
It is absorbed in the distal ileum before conversion to its active metabolite
items.rationale: Nabumetone is an enolic acid derivative (along with piroxicam and meloxicam) that is relatively nonacidic compared with most other NSAIDs, which accounts for its better gastrointestinal tolerance.

items.prompt: A 22-year-old patient is admitted to the emergency department 1 hour after ingesting an acute overdose of ibuprofen (40 tablets of 200 mg). The patient is lethargic and nauseated. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate as part of standard management for a nonsalicylate NSAID overdose?
options: Urgent hemodialysis to accelerate clearance of protein-bound ibuprofen
Administration of oral activated charcoal with supportive clinical care
Plotting a 6-hour serum ibuprofen concentration on the Done nomogram
Intravenous infusion of N-acetylcysteine using a weight-based protocol
items.rationale: Management of an acute overdose of a nonsalicylate NSAID (e.g., ibuprofen) consists of administering activated charcoal and providing supportive and symptomatic treatment. Unlike with salicylates, hemodialysis is of no value in enhancing the elimination of nonsalicylate NSAIDs, and the Done nomogram applies only to acute salicylate ingestion.

items.prompt: A patient with bipolar disorder maintained on lithium carbonate begins taking indomethacin for acute bursitis. Which laboratory abnormality and clinical risk should the nurse monitor for closely?
options: Elevated serum lithium concentrations and signs of lithium toxicity
Severe hypokalemia and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia on ECG
Prolonged prothrombin time and elevated international normalized ratio
Subtherapeutic serum lithium levels and acute manic symptom relapse
items.rationale: NSAIDs increase renal lithium reabsorption and reduce lithium clearance, resulting in increased serum lithium concentrations and a significant risk of lithium toxicity.

items.prompt: A kidney transplant recipient taking ciclosporin for immunosuppression asks the nurse if they can take naproxen for a sprained ankle. What is the primary hazard of combining an NSAID with ciclosporin?
options: Naproxen induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and triggers acute graft rejection
Ciclosporin competitively blocks naproxen binding at peripheral nociceptor sites
Combined therapy stimulates pancreatic beta cells and causes severe hypoglycemia
Renal prostaglandin inhibition potentiates ciclosporin nephrotoxicity and renal failure
items.rationale: When NSAIDs are taken with ciclosporin, inhibition of kidney prostaglandin synthesis potentiates the nephrotoxic effects of ciclosporin and can lead to acute kidney failure.

items.prompt: During a medication reconciliation, a patient taking meloxicam (Mobicox) daily for osteoarthritis reports taking several natural health products. Which group of herbal supplements interacts with NSAIDs to increase the risk of bleeding?
options: Feverfew, garlic, ginger, and ginkgo
Black cohosh, cranberry, and melatonin
Milk thistle, saw palmetto, and aloe
St. John's wort, valerian, and echinacea
items.rationale: Natural health products including feverfew, garlic, ginger, and ginkgo interfere with platelet function and interact with salicylates and other NSAIDs to increase bleeding risk.

items.prompt: A 66-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus and atrial fibrillation (treated with warfarin and metformin) starts taking over-the-counter glucosamine and chondroitin for knee osteoarthritis. Which monitoring parameters must be increased for this patient?
options: Serum potassium and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels
Serum uric acid and serum creatine kinase (CK) concentrations
International normalized ratio (INR) and blood glucose levels
Complete white blood cell differential and reticulocyte counts
items.rationale: Glucosamine and chondroitin can both enhance the anticoagulant effects of warfarin, requiring more frequent INR monitoring and possible warfarin dose adjustment. Additionally, glucosamine may increase insulin resistance, necessitating closer blood glucose monitoring and potentially higher dosages of oral hypoglycemics or insulin.

items.prompt: When educating a 78-year-old patient about starting a low-dose NSAID for osteoarthritis, which age-related physiological change in older adults explains why they may have higher serum drug levels and greater risk of gastrointestinal toxicity?
options: Increased cardiac output, accelerated hepatic metabolism, and alkaline gastric secretions
More acidic gastric juices, slower gastric motility, and reduced hepatic and renal blood flow
Hypertrophy of hepatic parenchyma and enhanced renal tubular secretion of organic acids
Increased total body water, elevated serum albumin binding, and rapid gastric emptying
items.rationale: Older adults experience a 25% decline in cardiac output (reducing renal blood flow and GFR), reduced liver size and hepatic blood flow (slowing metabolism), and GI changes including more acidic gastric juices and decreased gastric motility. These changes can lead to higher serum NSAID levels and increased risk of GI and renal toxicity.

items.prompt: A patient taking naproxen (Naprosyn) 500 mg twice daily for ankylosing spondylitis is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 3 weeks. What instruction should the nurse provide regarding the naproxen?
options: Continue taking naproxen until the morning of surgery to control postoperative pain
Consult the surgeon to discontinue naproxen at least 1 week before scheduled surgery
Switch from naproxen to regular-strength aspirin 48 hours before the surgical procedure
Withhold the naproxen starting 12 hours before surgery based on its elimination half-life
items.rationale: Because NSAIDs alter platelet function and increase the risk of perioperative bleeding, patients undergoing any elective surgery (including dental or minor surgery) should discontinue NSAIDs and aspirin at least 1 week prior to surgery per the prescriber's or surgeon's orders.

items.prompt: A patient with newly diagnosed hyperuricemia and gout asks the nurse how allopurinol (Zyloprim) works to prevent gout attacks. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: It binds proximal renal tubular transporters to increase urinary uric acid excretion
It inhibits xanthine oxidase to block conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid
It suppresses the mobility and chemotaxis of polymorphonuclear leukocytes in synovium
It hydrolyzes monosodium urate crystals already deposited within articular cartilage
items.rationale: Allopurinol (and its active metabolite oxypurinol) inhibits the enzyme xanthine oxidase, preventing the metabolic conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. It is indicated for patients who overproduce uric acid.

items.prompt: A patient who started taking allopurinol 3 weeks ago calls the clinic to report a new onset of fever, sore throat, malaise, and a painful, blistering skin rash that is peeling on the trunk. What is the nurse's priority action?
options: Reassure the patient that a mild photosensitive rash is expected and suggest hydrocortisone cream
Instruct the patient to stop allopurinol and seek urgent care for a severe cutaneous reaction
Advise taking allopurinol with meals and an oral antihistamine until the skin rash resolves
Recommend reducing the allopurinol dose by half and scheduling a clinic follow-up in 1 week
items.rationale: Allopurinol can cause serious and potentially fatal cutaneous hypersensitivity reactions, including exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), as well as agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia. Any skin rash or flu-like symptoms require immediate discontinuation and urgent medical assessment.

items.prompt: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a creatinine clearance (CrCl) of 15 mL/min and requires allopurinol for severe tophaceous gout. How should the allopurinol dosage be adjusted for this patient?
options: Administer the standard maximum dosage of 800 mg/day since elimination is biliary
Initiate therapy at 50 mg daily, titrate slowly, and do not exceed 200 mg/day
Administer 400 mg twice daily with probenecid to enhance renal oxypurinol clearance
Withhold allopurinol because it is contraindicated when CrCl falls below 30 mL/min
items.rationale: In renal impairment, allopurinol is not contraindicated, but doses should be initiated at 50 mg daily and titrated slowly with lower maximum doses: for CrCl 10–20 mL/min, the maximum dose is 200 mg/day, and for CrCl 3–10 mL/min, the maximum dose is 100 mg/day (compared with 800 mg/day in normal renal function).

items.prompt: A patient with lymphoma is scheduled to begin cytotoxic chemotherapy and is prescribed allopurinol. When should the allopurinol be initiated, and what is the rationale for its use?
options: Start a few days before chemotherapy to prevent hyperuricemia from tumour cell lysis
Start 48 hours after chemotherapy completion to accelerate bone marrow leukocyte recovery
Administer concurrently with mercaptopurine to potentiate antineoplastic cytotoxicity
Administer on an as-needed basis if acute podagra develops in the first metatarsophalangeal joint
items.rationale: Allopurinol is given a few days before starting chemotherapy to prevent acute tumour lysis syndrome—hyperuricemia and uric acid nephropathy resulting from massive purine release during rapid malignant cell lysis.

items.prompt: A patient taking febuxostat (Uloric) 80 mg/day for gout also has asthma and autoimmune hepatitis. Concomitant use of febuxostat or allopurinol with which medications is dangerous because xanthine oxidase inhibition markedly increases their toxicity?
options: Salbutamol, prednisone, or montelukast
Theophylline, azathioprine, or mercaptopurine
Metformin, levothyroxine, or atorvastatin
Amoxicillin, ciprofloxacin, or metronidazole
items.rationale: Azathioprine, mercaptopurine, and theophylline are metabolized by xanthine oxidase. Febuxostat is not to be given along with theophylline, azathioprine, or mercaptopurine, and allopurinol significantly interacts with azathioprine and mercaptopurine, requiring dosage adjustments to prevent severe toxicity.

items.prompt: A patient is prescribed oral colchicine for an acute gout flare with the following regimen: 1.2 mg initially, followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later, and then 0.6 mg every 2 hours. When should the patient stop taking the acute doses of colchicine?
options: After completing a full 7-day regimen to prevent recurrent urate crystal deposition
When serum uric acid concentrations fall below 200 µmol/L on repeat laboratory testing
Once mild tinnitus or visual blurring develops as an indicator of therapeutic saturation
When the acute joint pain subsides or when nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea first develops
items.rationale: For an acute gout flare, colchicine is given at 1 to 1.2 mg initially, followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later and every 2 hours until the gout pain disappears or until GI toxicity (nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea) develops. Furthermore, 3 days must pass before a second acute course is initiated.

items.prompt: A patient prescribed colchicine asks the nurse whether to take the tablets with meals or on an empty stomach. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: Chew the tablets with an antacid to prevent mucosal irritation in the esophagus
Take with a high-fat meal to dissolve the lipid-soluble coating of the tablet
Take on an empty stomach for optimal absorption, or with food if GI upset occurs
Take with grapefruit juice or an elixir to inhibit intestinal first-pass metabolism
items.rationale: According to the textbook, colchicine needs to be taken on an empty stomach for optimally complete absorption, although it is best tolerated if given with food when GI irritation is an issue. Patients must also avoid alcohol and OTC cold-relief products containing alcohol while taking colchicine.

items.prompt: A patient with chronic gout who underexcretes uric acid is prescribed probenecid (Benuryl) 250 mg PO twice daily for 1 week, then 500 mg twice daily. Which comorbidity in a patient's medical record would make probenecid ineffective or contraindicated?
options: Concomitant oral penicillin therapy for a soft-tissue bacterial infection
Peptic ulcer disease, hematological blood dyscrasias, or kidney impairment
Perennial allergic rhinitis or mild degenerative joint disease of the knees
Second-trimester pregnancy requiring maintenance uricosuric drug therapy
items.rationale: Contraindications to probenecid include peptic ulcer disease and blood dyscrasias. Furthermore, probenecid is ineffective in patients with kidney impairment and should not be used in these patients. (Conversely, probenecid is sometimes used therapeutically with penicillin to delay its renal excretion and prolong serum penicillin levels.)

items.prompt: A patient taking probenecid (Benuryl) for chronic gout reports taking over-the-counter acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) 650 mg twice daily for tension headaches. How should the nurse counsel the patient?
options: Discontinue ASA because salicylates antagonize probenecid and reduce uric acid excretion
Continue ASA because it acts synergistically with probenecid to alkalinize renal tubular urine
Administer ASA concurrently with probenecid to prevent uricosuric-induced auditory tinnitus
Switch from ASA to diflunisal because prescription salicylates prevent uric acid nephrolithiasis
items.rationale: Salicylates (such as ASA) antagonize the uricosuric mechanism of probenecid and sulfinpyrazone, resulting in decreased uric acid excretion and potential acute gout flares.

items.prompt: Which dietary and lifestyle teaching points should the nurse include for a patient prescribed allopurinol for chronic gout?
options: Follow a high-purine diet of organ meats and sardines to maintain xanthine oxidase activity
Take allopurinol on an empty stomach at bedtime with black coffee to prevent daytime sedation
Restrict fluid intake to 1 L/day to concentrate the drug in renal tubules and drink red wine
Take with meals, drink 3 L of fluid daily, avoid alcohol and caffeine, and limit high-purine foods
items.rationale: Patients taking allopurinol should take it with meals to minimize GI upset, increase fluid intake to 3 L/day (to maintain urine output of at least 2 L/day and prevent uric acid kidney stones), avoid alcohol and caffeine (which increase uric acid levels and decrease allopurinol levels), and limit high-purine foods (organ meats, seafood, meat extracts, yeast, beer, beans, peas, lentils, oatmeal, spinach, asparagus, cauliflower, mushrooms).

items.prompt: Which prostaglandin analogue medication may be co-prescribed to prevent serious gastrointestinal intolerance and peptic ulcers resulting from long-term NSAID therapy?
items.rationale: Misoprostol (Cytotec) is a synthetic prostaglandin analogue that replaces protective gastric prostaglandins depleted by COX-1 inhibition, preventing NSAID-induced gastric ulceration and mucosal injury.

items.prompt: What is the name of the standard graphic plot (originally published in 1960 in Pediatrics) that plots serum salicylate levels against time elapsed since ingestion (6 hours or longer) to estimate the severity of acute aspirin overdose?
items.rationale: The Done nomogram plots serum salicylate concentration as a function of time elapsed since an acute single salicylate ingestion (measured 6 hours or more post-ingestion) to gauge toxicity severity and guide treatment.

items.prompt: What is the single-word medical term for the syndrome of chronic salicylate toxicity, characterized in adults by tinnitus, hearing loss, nausea, and vomiting?
items.rationale: Salicylism is the syndrome of chronic salicylate intoxication resulting from short-term high dosages or prolonged therapy, commonly presenting with tinnitus, hearing loss, GI distress, and acid–base disturbances.

items.prompt: Which acute, potentially life-threatening condition involving encephalopathy and fatty degeneration of the liver is strongly associated with administering acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) to children or adolescents with viral illnesses such as influenza or chicken pox?
items.rationale: Reye's syndrome is an acute, life-threatening condition involving progressive neurological deficits (encephalopathy, cerebral edema, coma) and hepatic damage triggered by salicylate use during pediatric viral infections.

items.prompt: Name the selective cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitor currently remaining on the Canadian market.
items.rationale: Celecoxib (Celebrex) was the first COX-2 inhibitor approved and is the only one remaining on the Canadian market following the withdrawal of rofecoxib (Vioxx) and valdecoxib (Bextra).

items.prompt: Which enzyme is inhibited by both allopurinol (Zyloprim) and febuxostat (Uloric) to prevent the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid?
items.rationale: Allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit xanthine oxidase (XO), the enzyme responsible for converting hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid during purine metabolism.

items.prompt: What pharmacological class term describes drugs such as probenecid and sulfinpyrazone that inhibit renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid to promote its excretion in the urine?
items.rationale: Drugs that promote uric acid excretion in the urine by inhibiting its reabsorption in the proximal convoluted kidney tubule are known as uricosurics (e.g., probenecid, sulfinpyrazone).

items.prompt: Which acetic acid derivative NSAID (brand name Toradol) provides potent analgesia comparable to opioids such as morphine sulphate and is restricted to a maximum duration of 5 to 7 days?
items.rationale: Ketorolac tromethamine (Toradol) is an acetic acid derivative NSAID used for short-term management (maximum 5 days postsurgical or 7 days musculoskeletal) of moderate-to-severe acute pain.

items.prompt: What oral gastrointestinal decontamination agent is administered as first-line treatment for an acute overdose of a nonsalicylate NSAID such as ibuprofen?
items.rationale: For an acute overdose of a nonsalicylate NSAID, treatment consists of administering activated charcoal to prevent further GI absorption, followed by supportive and symptomatic care.

items.title: Tendinitis and NSAID-Induced Gastrointestinal Bleeding
items.scenario: Elena, a 38-year-old medical transcriptionist, presents to the outpatient clinic with severe pain and swelling in her right wrist that has prevented her from typing. Following physical examination and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), she is diagnosed with acute wrist tendinitis. She has no history of cardiovascular or kidney disease. The nurse practitioner prescribes extended-release diclofenac sodium (Voltaren-XR) 75 mg PO twice daily and fits her with a wrist splint.

question.prompt: Which administration instruction is most important for the nurse to include when teaching Elena about her new prescription for extended-release diclofenac (Voltaren-XR)?
options: Take on an empty stomach with black coffee to accelerate anti-inflammatory onset
Take an additional 75-mg tablet every 3 hours whenever wrist pain flares at work
Crush the tablets and mix them in applesauce to speed gastrointestinal absorption
Swallow the extended-release tablets whole with food or milk without crushing them
question.rationale: Sustained-release or enteric-coated NSAID formulations must never be crushed, broken, or chewed, and taking oral NSAIDs with food, milk, or antacids helps minimize gastrointestinal irritation.

stages.update: Five days after starting diclofenac-XR, Elena calls the clinic frustrated. She tells the nurse, 'The sharp pain is slightly duller for a few hours after I take a pill, but the swelling and stiffness in my wrist haven't gone away yet. Is this medication even working?'

question.prompt: What is the nurse's best therapeutic response to Elena's concern?
options: Remove the wrist splint and perform vigorous wrist exercises to enhance local drug delivery
Explain that analgesia begins early, but full anti-inflammatory effects take 1 week or longer
Add over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours until diclofenac reaches steady state
Discontinue diclofenac and request a corticosteroid injection since tendinitis resolves in 48 hours
question.rationale: When NSAIDs are used to decrease joint or tendon inflammation, full therapeutic anti-inflammatory effects may not be experienced for 1 week (7 days) or longer, even though mild analgesia occurs sooner. Combining two NSAIDs increases GI toxicity without added benefit.

stages.update: At her 1-month follow-up visit, Elena reports that her wrist pain and swelling have resolved and she has returned to work part-time. However, she mentions feeling unusually fatigued over the past week, experiencing gnawing epigastric discomfort, and noticing that her stools have become very dark and tarry. Her vital signs are BP 108/68 mmHg, HR 96 beats/min, RR 18 breaths/min. Laboratory results show hemoglobin 98 g/L (down from 134 g/L at baseline) and hematocrit 0.29.

question.prompt: How should the nurse interpret Elena's new clinical findings and laboratory values?
options: Benign stool discolouration from oxidized diclofenac metabolites in the gut
NSAID-induced upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding causing anemia
Subacute salicylate intoxication requiring evaluation on the Done nomogram
Acute reversible hepatotoxicity with cholestasis and impaired iron transport
question.rationale: Fatigue, epigastric discomfort, dark tarry stools (melena), tachycardia, and a drop in hemoglobin and hematocrit are classic indicators of NSAID-induced gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding resulting from COX-1 inhibition in the gastric mucosa.

stages.update: The nurse practitioner discontinues the diclofenac-XR and arranges endoscopic evaluation and iron supplementation. Elena asks how gastric ulcers from NSAIDs are prevented in patients who require anti-inflammatory therapy in the future.

question.prompt: Which medication strategy could the prescriber consider if anti-inflammatory therapy is required in a patient at high risk for NSAID-induced gastrointestinal toxicity?
options: Transitioning to parenteral ketorolac tromethamine for long-term maintenance therapy
Co-administering standardized ginkgo biloba and garlic extracts with each daily meal
Co-prescribing the prostaglandin analogue misoprostol or switching to oral celecoxib
Adding oral prednisone 20 mg daily to strengthen the protective gastric mucus barrier
question.rationale: Misoprostol (a prostaglandin analogue) may be given to prevent NSAID-induced GI intolerance and ulcers, or a selective COX-2 inhibitor (celecoxib) may be selected because it spares gastric COX-1 more than traditional nonselective NSAIDs. Corticosteroids and ketorolac increase ulcer risk.

items.title: Acute Gout Flare Transitioning to Chronic Urate-Lowering Therapy
items.scenario: Marcus, a 54-year-old chef with a BMI of 32 kg/m², presents to the urgent care clinic with excruciating pain, redness, heat, and swelling in his right first metatarsophalangeal (great toe) joint that woke him from sleep. He reports eating organ meats and shellfish and drinking several beers over the weekend. His serum uric acid level is elevated at 560 µmol/L, serum creatinine is 88 µmol/L, and eGFR is 82 mL/min. He is diagnosed with acute gouty arthritis (articular gout) and prescribed oral colchicine for the acute flare.

question.prompt: The nurse is educating Marcus on the acute colchicine dosing regimen (1.2 mg initially, followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later, and 0.6 mg every 2 hours). Which instruction is essential for safe administration during this acute attack?
options: Continue taking 0.6 mg every 2 hours for 5 full days even if watery diarrhea develops
Initiate a second acute colchicine course the next morning if mild toe pain persists
Stop taking the doses once joint pain resolves or if nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea occurs
Take the tablets with an alcohol-based elixir or beer to promote sleep during the flare
question.rationale: During an acute gout flare, colchicine is administered until the gout pain disappears or until GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea) develop. At least 3 days must elapse before a second acute course of therapy is initiated, and alcohol must be avoided.

stages.update: After taking three doses of colchicine, Marcus's toe pain begins to subside, but he develops two loose stools and mild abdominal cramping. He stops the acute regimen as instructed. Two days later, he calls the clinic to report that his urine looks pink-tinged and smoky, and he feels unusually lethargic and feverish.
