question.rationale: Combination products (such as OTC cough and cold remedies and prescription opioid combinations) account for more than half of all acetaminophen doses sold in Canada. Patients must read all product labels carefully to avoid exceeding the maximum recommended daily limit (4 000 mg/day in healthy adults, or 2 000 mg/day with alcohol/liver risk factors).

items.title: Geriatric Postherpetic Neuralgia, Polypharmacy, and Renal Impairment
items.topic: Analgesics: Special Populations: Older Adults & Miscellaneous Analgesics
items.scenario: Mr. Arthur Pendelton, a 78-year-old man, presents to the primary care clinic with severe burning, stabbing pain along his left thoracic dermatome 6 weeks after a resolved outbreak of shingles (herpes zoster). His medical history includes depression (treated with sertraline, an SSRI), benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and stage 3 chronic kidney disease (serum creatinine 165 µmol/L). The skin over his left chest is now fully healed and intact without blisters.

question.prompt: A medical resident suggests prescribing tramadol hydrochloride (Ultram) 100 mg PO every 6 hours for Mr. Pendelton's postherpetic neuralgia. Why should the nurse advocate against this prescription?
options: Tramadol is avoided at age 75 or older, and combining it with sertraline raises the risk of seizures and serotonin syndrome
Tramadol acts as a competitive opioid antagonist at dorsal horn mu receptors and exacerbates postherpetic neuropathic pain
Tramadol requires parenteral administration in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia due to poor intestinal absorption
Tramadol reactivates dormant varicella-zoster virus in dorsal root ganglia and triggers recurrent vesicular skin eruptions
question.rationale: Tramadol is not recommended for individuals 75 years of age or older. Furthermore, because tramadol inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake and lowers the seizure threshold, coadministration with an SSRI like sertraline carries a significant risk of serotonin syndrome and seizures.

stages.update: The prescriber agrees and instead orders transdermal lidocaine patches to be applied to the painful area on Mr. Pendelton's left chest, along with low-dose pregabalin as an adjuvant for neuropathic pain.

question.prompt: Which instruction must the nurse give Mr. Pendelton regarding the safe application of his transdermal lidocaine patches?
options: Apply patches to intact skin for up to 12 hours per 24-hour period to prevent systemic lidocaine toxicity and dysrhythmias
Leave up to three lidocaine patches in place continuously for 72 hours before rotating to a fresh thoracic skin site
Place a warm heating pad over the thoracic patches for 30 minutes twice daily to enhance penetration into intercostal nerves
Reapply the same patches for up to 5 consecutive mornings as long as the adhesive edges remain intact on the chest wall
question.rationale: Transdermal lidocaine patches are indicated for postherpetic neuralgia on intact skin. Up to three patches may be applied to a large painful area, but they must not be worn for longer than 12 hours in a 24-hour period to prevent systemic absorption and toxicity (such as cardiac dysrhythmias).

stages.update: Two months later, Mr. Pendelton is admitted to the orthopedic unit with an acute intertrochanteric hip fracture after slipping on ice. He requires parenteral opioid analgesia prior to surgical repair.

question.prompt: Given Mr. Pendelton's age (78 years) and impaired kidney function (creatinine 165 µmol/L), which opioid selection and dosing strategy is safest?
options: Start a lower IV dose of hydromorphone or fentanyl and titrate slowly, avoiding morphine and meperidine in kidney disease
Administer scheduled intramuscular meperidine 100 mg every 3 hours because normeperidine is cleared via biliary excretion
Apply a 50 mcg/hr transdermal fentanyl patch preoperatively to achieve rapid steady-state analgesia before hip surgery
Administer standard adult doses of intravenous morphine sulphate because reduced glomerular filtration prolongs analgesia safely
question.rationale: In older adults with kidney impairment, morphine (active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide) and meperidine (active neurotoxic metabolite normeperidine) should be avoided because their metabolites accumulate in renal insufficiency. Hydromorphone or IV fentanyl started at a lower dose and titrated slowly is safer. Transdermal fentanyl is contraindicated for acute pain and in opioid-naive patients.

stages.update: Following hip surgery, Mr. Pendelton is receiving low-dose IV hydromorphone. Due to his history of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), the nurse closely monitors his genitourinary status and fall risk.

question.prompt: Which nursing assessment parameter and safety measure are priorities for Mr. Pendelton while he receives opioid therapy?
options: Monitor for urinary retention (output at least 720 mL/24 hr) given his BPH, and maintain fall precautions with bed alarms
Have him ambulate unassisted to the bathroom 30 minutes after each IV hydromorphone dose to evaluate orthostatic tolerance
Anticipate osmotic diuresis exceeding 3 500 mL/24 hr as hydromorphone relaxes internal urethral sphincter smooth muscle
Wait for Mr. Pendelton to request analgesia spontaneously because older adults commonly overreport postoperative pain
question.rationale: In older adult males with BPH, opioid-induced increases in bladder sphincter tone can precipitate acute urinary retention; urine output should be monitored to ensure at least 720 mL/24 hr. Older adults are often stoic or reluctant to bother the nurse about pain, and are at high risk for CNS depression, orthostatic hypotension, and falls—requiring call bells within reach and bed alarms.

items.title: Pediatric Appendectomy Pain Assessment and Safe Dosing
items.topic: Analgesics: Special Populations: Children & Analgesic Dosing
items.scenario: Leo Martinez, a 6-year-old boy weighing 20 kg, is admitted to the pediatric surgical unit following a laparoscopic appendectomy. He is awake, crying, guarding his abdomen, and afraid to move in bed, but tells his mother he 'doesn't hurt' because he is terrified of getting a needle.

question.prompt: Which pain assessment approach and nursing action are most appropriate for evaluating Leo's pain?
options: Use the Wong-Baker FACES scale (0 to 5), observe nonverbal cues with parent input, and explain needle-free IV dosing
Accept his verbal denial of pain at face value, document a score of 0/10, and withhold analgesics to avoid oversedation
Ask him to complete the written adult McGill Pain Questionnaire independently to localize his abdominal discomfort
Explain that he must receive an intramuscular deltoid injection if he continues crying and guarding his abdomen
question.rationale: Children often deny pain out of fear of injections. Nurses must assess both verbal and nonverbal cues (guarding, crying, rigidity, fear of moving), involve parents, use age-appropriate tools like the Wong-Baker 'OUCH' FACES scale (for children 3 years and older, rated 0 to 5), and use oral or IV routes rather than traumatic IM injections.

stages.update: Using the FACES scale, Leo points to the tearful face (level 5) once he learns his medicine can be given through his existing IV line without a needle stick. The surgeon orders morphine sulphate 0.1 mg/kg IV every 4 hours as needed for severe pain.

question.prompt: Leo weighs 20 kg and the ordered dose is 0.1 mg/kg. How many milligrams (mg) of morphine sulphate should the nurse administer for a single dose? (Enter the number and unit, e.g., 2 mg)
question.rationale: Pediatric morphine dosing must be calculated carefully by body weight: 20 kg × 0.1 mg/kg = 2 mg per dose.

stages.update: Thirty minutes after receiving the 2 mg IV dose of morphine sulphate, the nurse reassesses Leo. Which clinical finding would require the nurse to withhold further opioid doses and notify the physician immediately?

question.prompt: Which assessment finding indicates a serious opioid adverse effect in this pediatric patient?
options: Sluggish pupillary light reflex, new lethargy or altered consciousness, or a respiratory rate below 10 breaths/min
Heart rate decreasing from 118 beats/min to 94 beats/min as his postoperative crying and abdominal guarding subside
Pointing to face level 1 on the Wong-Baker FACES scale and asking his mother if he can watch television in bed
Blood pressure decreasing from 112/72 mm Hg to 100/64 mm Hg while resting quietly with warm, pink extremities
question.rationale: In children receiving opioids, CNS changes such as drowsiness/lethargy, hallucinations, changes in level of consciousness, sluggish pupil reaction, or respiratory depression (respiratory rate <10 breaths/min) must be reported to the physician immediately and further opioid doses withheld.

stages.update: On postoperative day 2, Leo is tolerating a regular diet and is ready for discharge home with oral pain medication. His mother asks if the surgeon can prescribe codeine syrup, or if she can give him adult aspirin tablets from home if he gets a fever.

question.prompt: Which discharge teaching by the nurse is accurate regarding pediatric analgesics?
options: Avoid codeine (CYP2D6 toxicity risk) and aspirin (Reye's syndrome risk); give weight-based acetaminophen with a dosing device
Administer over-the-counter codeine cough syrup every 4 hours with food to prevent postoperative nausea and stomach upset
Give chewable aspirin tablets every 6 hours as the antipyretic of choice if he develops a low-grade postoperative fever
Quarter an adult extended-release oxycodone tablet and dissolve it in apple juice to provide 12 hours of abdominal pain relief
question.rationale: Health Canada recommends against using codeine in children and youth under 18 years of age due to the risk of fatal toxicity in ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers. Aspirin is avoided in children and adolescents due to the risk of Reye's syndrome. Weight-based acetaminophen (15 mg/kg/dose PO q4–6h PRN, max 5 doses or 75 mg/kg/day) measured with an accurate dosing device is appropriate.

items.prompt: A nurse is preparing to administer a scheduled morning dose of oral digoxin 0.125 mg to a patient with heart failure. Which nursing assessment is the priority before giving this medication?
options: Auscultate the apical pulse at the fifth intercostal space for 1 full minute
Palpate the radial and brachial pulses bilaterally for 30 seconds to compare
Measure orthostatic blood pressure in the supine and standing positions
Assess the point of maximal impulse and check for jugular venous distension
items.rationale: Before administering any dose of digoxin, the nurse must auscultate the apical pulse at the left midclavicular line, fifth intercostal space, for 1 full minute to detect bradycardia, tachycardia, or irregular rhythms. Radial palpation for 30 seconds can miss rhythm irregularities and pulse deficits.

items.prompt: A patient with heart failure has an order for digoxin 0.25 mg PO daily. Upon assessment, the nurse auscultates an apical heart rate of 54 beats/min and notes the patient reports mild nausea. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Administer the digoxin with a light snack and recheck the pulse in 1 hour
Withhold the scheduled digoxin dose and contact the health care provider
Give half the prescribed tablet and obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram now
Prepare an intravenous infusion of digoxin immune Fab over a 30-minute period
items.rationale: When the apical pulse is 60 beats/min or lower (or greater than 100 beats/min), or when signs of digoxin toxicity such as nausea are present, the nurse should withhold the dose and contact the health care provider. Digoxin immune Fab is reserved for life-threatening toxicity.

items.prompt: How does digoxin produce a positive inotropic effect in a patient with systolic heart failure?
options: By stimulating myocardial beta-1 adrenergic receptors to increase cyclic AMP
By inhibiting phosphodiesterase type III in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle
By inhibiting the sodium–potassium ATPase pump to raise intracellular calcium
By blocking voltage-gated potassium channels to prolong ventricular repolarization
items.rationale: Digoxin inhibits the sodium–potassium adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) pump, leading to increased intracellular sodium and calcium concentrations, which enhances myocardial contractility (positive inotropic effect). Beta-1 stimulation describes dobutamine, and PDE-III inhibition describes milrinone.

items.prompt: A student nurse asks the preceptor to explain the negative chronotropic and negative dromotropic effects of digoxin. Which explanation by the preceptor is accurate?
options: Digoxin accelerates sinoatrial firing and speeds Purkinje fibre conduction
Digoxin dilates coronary vessels and shortens the atrial refractory period
Digoxin decreases stroke volume while increasing sympathetic nodal outflow
Digoxin slows heart rate via vagal tone and delays AV nodal conduction
items.rationale: A negative chronotropic effect reduces heart rate (partly by augmenting vagal tone), and a negative dromotropic effect decreases conduction velocity through the AV node and prolongs the refractory period.

items.prompt: A patient taking digoxin and furosemide for heart failure presents to the clinic reporting fatigue, anorexia, and seeing yellowish-green halos around lights. Which laboratory result most likely precipitated these symptoms?
options: Serum potassium of 2.9 mmol/L
Serum sodium of 140 mmol/L
Serum magnesium of 0.95 mmol/L
Serum creatinine of 75 µmol/L
items.rationale: Hypokalemia (serum potassium < 3.5 mmol/L), often caused by loop diuretics like furosemide, strongly predisposes patients to digoxin toxicity, manifested by anorexia, fatigue, and yellow-green halo vision. The other laboratory values are within normal limits.

items.prompt: According to the 2017 Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines, what is the recommended role of digoxin in the management of chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)?
options: First-line monotherapy for newly diagnosed patients to reduce 5-year mortality
Adjunctive therapy for patients in sinus rhythm with persistent severe symptoms
Routine prophylactic therapy for Stage A patients with hypertension and diabetes
Primary maintenance therapy for patients with isolated diastolic dysfunction
items.rationale: Digoxin is no longer a first-line drug and does not reduce mortality; it is recommended for patients with HFrEF in normal sinus rhythm who continue to have moderate-to-severe symptoms despite optimized therapy (ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta blockers, diuretics) to relieve symptoms and reduce hospitalizations.

items.prompt: A patient with atrial fibrillation and heart failure has just been started on amiodarone in addition to long-term oral digoxin therapy. What modification to the plan of care should the nurse anticipate?
options: Increasing the daily digoxin dose by 50% due to enhanced renal drug clearance
Spacing the two medications 2 hours apart to prevent gastrointestinal binding
Reducing the daily digoxin dose by 50% due to decreased digoxin clearance
Switching oral digoxin to an equivalent intravenous dose during concurrent therapy
items.rationale: Amiodarone, quinidine, and verapamil decrease digoxin clearance and can increase serum digoxin levels by approximately 50%; therefore, the digoxin dose should be reduced by 50% to prevent toxicity.

items.prompt: During a home visit, a patient taking oral digoxin tells the nurse about several new dietary habits and natural health products. Which product reported by the patient increases the risk of digoxin toxicity by causing potassium loss?
options: Omega-3 fatty acid capsules
St. John's wort extract
Toasted wheat bran muffins
Natural black licorice
items.rationale: Licorice increases the risk of digoxin cardiac toxicity due to potassium loss (hypokalemia). St. John's wort and wheat bran decrease digoxin levels/absorption, while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids are recommended as safe adjunctive therapy in heart failure.

items.prompt: A patient asks why they should avoid taking their morning digoxin tablet with a large bowl of bran cereal or an antacid. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: Bran and antacids bind oral digoxin in the gut and decrease its absorption
High-fibre foods and antacids inhibit hepatic enzymes and raise drug levels
Combining digoxin with antacids accelerates gastric emptying and causes cramps
Dietary fibre and antacids increase renal tubular reabsorption of the medication
items.rationale: High-fibre foods (such as bran), dairy products, and antacids interfere with and decrease the oral absorption and bioavailability of digoxin. Patients should avoid taking them within 2 hours before or after their heart failure medications.

items.prompt: A nurse is teaching a patient discharged on digoxin 0.125 mg PO once daily at 0800. Which statement by the patient indicates correct understanding of what to do if a dose is missed?
options: If I forget a morning dose, I should take two tablets the next morning at 0800.
If less than 12 hours have passed, I can still take the missed dose that day.
If I miss my 0800 dose by more than 2 hours, I must skip it until tomorrow.
If I feel short of breath in the evening, I can take an extra half-tablet dose.
items.rationale: If a dose of digoxin is missed, the patient may take it if no more than 12 hours have passed since the scheduled time. If more than 12 hours have elapsed, the patient should skip the missed dose, not double the next dose, and contact the health care provider.

items.prompt: Which medication order for digoxin complies with Institute for Safe Medication Practices (ISMP) Canada guidelines to prevent 10-fold or 100-fold dosing errors?
options: Digoxin 1.0 mg PO once daily
Digoxin .25 mg PO once daily
Digoxin 0.25 mg PO once daily
Digoxin .125 mg PO once daily
items.rationale: ISMP Canada states that leading zeros must be used before a decimal point for doses less than a whole number (0.25 mg, not .25 mg) and trailing zeros must not be used after a decimal point (1 mg, not 1.0 mg) to prevent lethal decimal-point misreadings.

items.prompt: The nurse is preparing to administer intravenous digoxin 0.25 mg to a hospitalized patient with acute heart failure. How should the nurse safely administer this medication?
options: Administer as a rapid intravenous bolus over 30 seconds followed by normal saline
Combine with intravenous furosemide in the same syringe and infuse over 2 minutes
Dilute in 250 mL of 5% dextrose in water and infuse over 4 hours via gravity drip
Infuse undiluted slowly over at least 5 minutes at a rate up to 0.25 mg/minute
items.rationale: Intravenous digoxin should be infused undiluted at approximately 0.25 mg per minute, over longer than a 5-minute period (or per hospital protocol), and must not be mixed with incompatible medications in the same syringe or solution.

items.prompt: For which patient with suspected digoxin toxicity is the administration of digoxin immune Fab clinically indicated?
options: A patient with serum potassium of 5.6 mmol/L and sustained ventricular tachycardia
A patient with a serum digoxin level of 2.1 ng/mL reporting fatigue and anorexia
A patient with an apical heart rate of 56 beats/min and a potassium of 4.1 mmol/L
A patient with chronic kidney disease who took an extra 0.125-mg tablet this morning
items.rationale: Digoxin immune Fab is reserved for severe, life-threatening toxicity: hyperkalemia (serum potassium > 5 mmol/L) in a toxic patient, life-threatening dysrhythmias (sustained ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation or severe bradycardia/heart block unresponsive to atropine or pacing), or massive overdose (> 10 mg in adults or > 4 mg in children).

items.prompt: A patient with a life-threatening digoxin overdose receives intravenous digoxin immune Fab. Twelve hours later, a repeat total serum digoxin level is drawn and reported as markedly elevated. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: The antidote dose was insufficient, and a repeat bolus of Fab fragments is needed
Standard assays measure bound and free drug, so clinical status guides monitoring
Enterohepatic recirculation has released unbound digoxin back into the bloodstream
Renal clearance of the antigen–antibody complex has stalled due to tubular injury
items.rationale: After digoxin immune Fab is administered, subsequent serum digoxin measurements will be elevated for days to weeks because standard assays measure both free and Fab-bound digoxin. Clinical signs, ECG rhythm, and potassium levels must guide evaluation of reversal effectiveness.

items.prompt: Before administering digoxin immune Fab to a patient with severe digoxin toxicity, the nurse reviews the patient's allergy history. An allergy to which substance places the patient at highest risk for an anaphylactic reaction to digoxin immune Fab?
options: Egg albumin, feathers, or soybean oil
Shellfish, kelp, or iodinated contrast
Papaya extracts, papain, or sheep protein
Horse serum, gelatin, or neomycin sulfate
items.rationale: Digoxin immune Fab is produced from immunoglobulin fragments obtained from sheep immunized with a digoxin derivative and cleaved using papain. Patients allergic to papaya, papain, or sheep (ovine) protein must be monitored closely for anaphylactic shock.

items.prompt: A patient has ingested 6 mg of digoxin in an acute overdose, and the health care provider orders digoxin immune Fab to neutralize the ingested drug. Knowing that one vial of digoxin immune Fab binds 0.5 mg of digoxin, how many vials will the nurse prepare?
options: 24 vials
15 vials
6 vials
12 vials
items.rationale: One vial of digoxin immune Fab binds 0.5 mg of digoxin. To neutralize 6 mg of digoxin: 6 mg ÷ 0.5 mg/vial = 12 vials.

items.prompt: The pharmacy delivers reconstituted vials of digoxin immune Fab to the intensive care unit for a patient in third-degree heart block from digoxin toxicity. Which storage and handling guideline must the nurse follow?
options: Administer the mixed solution promptly or discard it within 4 hours
Keep the reconstituted solution at room temperature for up to 24 hours
Protect the diluted solution from light and infuse over 4 to 6 hours
Warm the refrigerated vials to body temperature before reconstitution
items.rationale: Unreconstituted vials of digoxin immune Fab should be refrigerated, and once mixed, the solution is stable for 4 hours; it must be used promptly or discarded after 4 hours. It is normally infused over 30 minutes unless cardiac arrest is imminent.

items.prompt: Why is the phosphodiesterase inhibitor milrinone classified as an 'inodilator' in the treatment of heart failure?
options: It slows sinoatrial node firing while constricting peripheral venous vessels
It increases myocardial contractility while dilating vascular smooth muscle
It blocks renal aldosterone receptors while inhibiting angiotensin-converting enzyme
It stimulates myocardial beta-1 receptors while blocking peripheral alpha-1 tone
items.rationale: Milrinone inhibits phosphodiesterase type III, increasing intracellular cAMP in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle. This produces both a positive inotropic effect (stronger contraction) and vasodilation (reduced afterload), earning the term 'inodilator'.

items.prompt: A patient in the intensive care unit is receiving a continuous intravenous infusion of milrinone for acute heart failure. Which primary adverse effect requires continuous electrocardiographic (ECG) monitoring?
options: Atrioventricular nodal block
Sinoatrial arrest and pauses
Ventricular dysrhythmias
Refractory sinus bradycardia
items.rationale: The primary adverse effect of milrinone therapy is cardiac dysrhythmia—specifically ventricular dysrhythmias, which occur in approximately 12% of treated patients. Continuous ECG monitoring in a critical care setting is essential.

items.prompt: A patient is receiving a continuous intravenous infusion of milrinone via a central venous line. The health care provider orders furosemide 40 mg IV stat for pulmonary crackles. Which action by the nurse is essential?
options: Withhold the furosemide while the patient receives a phosphodiesterase inhibitor
Slow the milrinone infusion by half while injecting furosemide into the Y-site
Dilute the furosemide in 100 mL of normal saline before piggybacking into the line
Administer the furosemide through a separate IV line to avoid chemical precipitation
items.rationale: Parenteral furosemide must not be injected into intravenous lines containing milrinone because a chemical precipitation occurs on contact. A separate compatible IV access or thoroughly flushed separate lumen must be used.

items.prompt: A patient receiving an intravenous milrinone infusion develops a blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg and reports dizziness. Which action should the nurse anticipate taking?
options: Reduce or temporarily stop the milrinone infusion and notify the prescriber
Administer intravenous calcium gluconate to counteract the vasodilatory effect
Increase the milrinone rate slightly to improve left ventricular stroke volume
Elevate the head of the bed to 90 degrees and administer oral midodrine stat
items.rationale: No specific antidote exists for milrinone overdose, and hypotension secondary to vasodilation is the primary manifestation. If excessive hypotension occurs, the infusion rate should be reduced or temporarily stopped until the patient stabilizes, and the prescriber notified.

items.prompt: In addition to ECG rhythm and blood pressure, which hematologic laboratory parameter should the nurse monitor closely in a patient receiving milrinone?
options: Hemoglobin and hematocrit for hemolytic anemia
Platelet count for thrombocytopenia
White blood cell count for agranulocytosis
Prothrombin time for factor VII deficiency
items.rationale: Thrombocytopenia is a recognized adverse effect of milrinone therapy, along with ventricular dysrhythmias, hypotension, angina, hypokalemia, headache, tremor, and elevated liver enzymes.

items.prompt: An adult patient weighing 80 kg is prescribed an intravenous loading dose of milrinone at 50 mcg/kg. How many milligrams of milrinone will the nurse administer for the loading dose?
options: 40 mg
0.4 mg
4 mg
2.5 mg
items.rationale: Loading dose = 50 mcg/kg × 80 kg = 4 000 mcg. Converting micrograms to milligrams: 4 000 mcg ÷ 1 000 = 4 mg.

items.prompt: How do angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors such as lisinopril improve cardiac function in a patient with heart failure?
options: They stimulate renal prostaglandins to enhance glomerular filtration pressure
They block cardiac beta-1 receptors to prolong ventricular diastolic filling time
They inhibit the sodium–potassium pump to increase intracellular calcium stores
They inhibit angiotensin II and aldosterone, reducing preload and LV remodeling
items.rationale: ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, preventing potent vasoconstriction and inhibiting aldosterone-mediated sodium and water resorption. This decreases preload (LVEDV), reduces cardiac workload, and slows adverse left ventricular remodeling.

items.prompt: A patient who started lisinopril 3 weeks ago for heart failure calls the clinic reporting an annoying, dry, nonproductive cough. The patient's lungs are clear to auscultation, weight is stable, and oxygen saturation is 98%. What causes this adverse effect?
options: Accumulation of insoluble bradykinins in the bronchi from ACE inhibition
Mild pulmonary venous congestion caused by nocturnal fluid redistribution
Reflex vagal stimulation of the upper airway triggered by arterial dilation
Bronchial smooth muscle constriction due to beta-2 adrenergic blockade
items.rationale: ACE inhibitors can cause a harmless but annoying dry cough because insoluble bradykinins (by-products of ACE inhibition) build up in the blood and lodge in the bronchial tubes. If intolerable, the patient may be switched to an ARB such as valsartan.

items.prompt: A nurse is reviewing the medication profile and laboratory results of a patient taking lisinopril for heart failure. Which finding requires prompt follow-up with the prescriber?
options: Blood pressure of 116/72 mm Hg measured 6 hours after the morning lisinopril dose
Serum potassium level of 5.8 mmol/L while taking a daily potassium supplement
Apical heart rate of 68 beats/min with a regular sinus rhythm on telemetry
Serum creatinine of 88 µmol/L and blood urea nitrogen within the reference range
items.rationale: Because ACE inhibitors suppress aldosterone secretion, they can cause hyperkalemia. A serum potassium of 5.8 mmol/L is dangerously elevated, and concurrent potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics must be used with caution or discontinued.

items.topic: Heart failure: Angiotensin II receptor blockers
items.prompt: A patient with heart failure is switched from lisinopril to valsartan due to a persistent dry cough. How does valsartan differ from lisinopril in its adverse effect profile?
options: Valsartan produces a positive inotropic effect without altering blood pressure
Valsartan can be safely continued during pregnancy without fetal renal toxicity
Valsartan is less likely to cause a bradykinin-mediated cough or hyperkalemia
Valsartan increases systemic vascular resistance while reducing venous preload
items.rationale: Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) such as valsartan decrease systemic vascular resistance (afterload) like ACE inhibitors, but they are much less likely to cause the bradykinin-mediated dry cough or hyperkalemia. Like ACE inhibitors, ARBs are teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy.

items.topic: Heart failure: ACE inhibitors and ARBs
items.prompt: A 32-year-old woman with cardiomyopathy and chronic heart failure tells the nurse that she and her partner are planning a pregnancy. She currently takes valsartan and metoprolol. Which information is essential for the nurse to share?
options: Abruptly discontinue both medications at home as soon as a pregnancy test is positive
Continue valsartan during the first trimester and switch to lisinopril in the second
Reduce the valsartan dose by half before conception to prevent maternal hypotension
Consult the prescriber before conception to replace valsartan due to fetal toxicity
items.rationale: Both ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril) and ARBs (e.g., valsartan) cause fetal and neonatal morbidity and death when used during pregnancy. The patient must consult her health care provider to transition to safer therapy before conceiving.

items.prompt: Which three beta blockers have been shown in clinical trials to reduce mortality in patients with heart failure?
options: Bisoprolol, extended-release metoprolol, and carvedilol
Propranolol, immediate-release atenolol, and sotalol
Labetalol, sustained-release propranolol, and pindolol
Esmolol, extended-release nadolol, and acebutolol
items.rationale: According to heart failure guidelines and textbook evidence, the three beta blockers proven to reduce mortality in heart failure are bisoprolol, extended-release metoprolol, and carvedilol.

items.prompt: A patient with heart failure asks why a beta blocker such as metoprolol is prescribed when the heart is already weak. Which explanation by the nurse best describes the cardioprotective mechanism of beta blockers?
options: It increases intracellular calcium availability to strengthen ventricular contraction
It blocks sympathetic catecholamine stimulation to reduce heart rate and workload
It inhibits renal tubular sodium reabsorption to decrease intravascular fluid volume
It dilates systemic arterioles directly by opening vascular potassium channels
items.rationale: Beta blockers protect the failing heart by blocking sympathetic nervous system (catecholamine) stimulation, which reduces heart rate, delays AV node conduction, decreases myocardial automaticity, and helps preserve left ventricular function and reverse remodeling.

items.prompt: How does carvedilol differ pharmacologically from cardioselective beta blockers like metoprolol and bisoprolol in the treatment of mild-to-moderate heart failure?
options: Carvedilol selectively stimulates beta-2 receptors to prevent bronchoconstriction
Carvedilol possesses intrinsic sympathomimetic activity that maintains heart rate
Carvedilol acts as a nonselective beta blocker, alpha-1 blocker, and antioxidant
Carvedilol blocks renal mineralocorticoid receptors in addition to beta-1 receptors
items.rationale: Carvedilol is an oral nonselective beta blocker that also blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors (causing vasodilation) and possesses possible calcium channel blocking and antioxidant properties, slowing heart failure progression and reducing hospitalizations.

items.prompt: As a patient's heart failure progresses to a more severe stage, the cardiologist adds eplerenone to the regimen of lisinopril, carvedilol, and furosemide. What is the therapeutic action of eplerenone?
options: It inhibits neprilysin to increase endogenous natriuretic peptide concentrations
It inhibits phosphodiesterase type III to enhance cardiac relaxation and output
It blocks funny-channel sodium currents in the sinoatrial node to slow heart rate
It selectively blocks aldosterone receptors in the kidneys, heart, and vessels
items.rationale: Eplerenone (Inspra) and spironolactone (Aldactone) are aldosterone antagonists (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) added in severe stages of heart failure to block aldosterone-mediated sodium and water retention and worsening heart failure.

items.topic: Heart failure: Vasodilators in heart failure
items.prompt: A combination of hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate is specifically recommended in heart failure treatment guidelines for which patient population?
options: Patients with heart failure who are Black
Patients with congenital septal defects
Patients with severe aortic stenosis
Patients with right ventricular failure
items.rationale: The combination of hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate is specifically approved and recommended in clinical guidelines for patients with heart failure who are Black.

items.topic: Heart failure: Vasodilators in heart failure
items.prompt: A patient is receiving the first few doses of hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate for heart failure. Which nursing intervention and patient teaching is most important?
options: Limit dietary sodium and potassium intake to prevent hyperkalemic dysrhythmias
Monitor blood pressure closely and advise slow position changes due to syncope risk
Assess colour vision and pupillary reflexes hourly for signs of nitrate neurotoxicity
Give the medications with dairy products to delay peak plasma levels beyond 4 hours
items.rationale: Hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate reach peak plasma levels in 1 hour and must be used with caution because of the risk of syncope and hypotension, especially with the first few doses. Patients should be taught to change positions carefully.

items.prompt: A patient is admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit in acute decompensated heart failure with hemodynamic instability. The prescriber orders a continuous intravenous infusion of dobutamine. How does dobutamine improve cardiac output?
options: By activating vascular alpha-1 receptors to raise systemic arterial blood pressure
By inhibiting parasympathetic vagal tone to accelerate atrioventricular conduction
By stimulating myocardial beta-1 receptors to increase contractility and output
By sensitizing cardiac troponin C to calcium without increasing oxygen consumption
items.rationale: Dobutamine hydrochloride is a beta-1-selective vasoactive adrenergic agonist structurally similar to dopamine. By stimulating myocardial beta-1 receptors, it increases contractility (positive inotropy), stroke volume, and cardiac output in acute decompensated heart failure.

items.topic: Heart failure: Adjunctive heart failure therapy
items.prompt: According to the 2017 Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines, which natural health product is recommended as adjunctive therapy in chronic heart failure to help reduce mortality and hospital admissions?
options: Standardized hawthorn leaf extract 300 mg twice daily
Siberian ginseng root extract 500 mg taken twice daily
Coenzyme Q10 ubiquinone capsules 200 mg once daily
Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) 1 g daily
items.rationale: The 2017 Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines recommend 1 g daily of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs; containing 850 to 882 mg of EPA and DHA as ethyl esters in a 1:1.2 ratio) as adjunctive therapy to reduce mortality and hospitalizations in chronic heart failure.

items.prompt: A patient with chronic heart failure undergoes an echocardiogram that reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35%. According to the 2017 Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines, how is this patient's heart failure classified?
options: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
Heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction (HFmEF)
Heart failure with recovered ejection fraction (HFrecEF)
items.rationale: According to the 2017 CCS guidelines, an LVEF ≤ 40% is classified as heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), 41%–49% is mid-range (HFmEF), and ≥ 50% is preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Normal EF is approximately 65%.

items.prompt: A patient with structural heart disease experiences marked limitation in normal physical activity; walking across the room causes fatigue and dyspnea, though the patient is comfortable at rest. Which New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class describes this patient?
options: NYHA Functional Class I
NYHA Functional Class III
NYHA Functional Class II
NYHA Functional Class IV
items.rationale: NYHA Class III is characterized by a marked limitation in normal physical activity. Class I has no limitation, Class II has symptoms with ordinary physical activity, and Class IV has symptoms at rest or with any physical activity.

items.prompt: A nurse is assessing a 4-month-old infant admitted with heart failure secondary to a congenital septal defect. Which clinical manifestations are most characteristic of heart failure in an infant?
options: Dependent ankle edema while upright, jugular venous distension, and orthopnea
Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, dry hacking cough, and frothy pink-tinged sputum
Difficulty feeding, poor weight gain, diaphoresis during feeds, and tachypnea
Ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, bounding peripheral pulses, and sinus bradycardia
items.rationale: In infants and young children, heart failure typically manifests as poor growth, feeding difficulties (reflux, vomiting, feeding refusal), diaphoresis, pallor, and tachypnea, most commonly caused by congenital heart defects.

items.prompt: A 6-year-old child weighing 22 kg is prescribed a single oral dose of digoxin elixir at 15 mcg/kg. How many milligrams of digoxin should the nurse administer?
options: 3.3 mg
1.5 mg
items.rationale: Dose in micrograms = 15 mcg/kg × 22 kg = 330 mcg. Convert micrograms to milligrams by dividing by 1 000: 330 mcg ÷ 1 000 = 0.33 mg. Careful decimal placement prevents a lethal 10-fold dosing error.

items.topic: Heart failure: Patient teaching in heart failure
items.prompt: The nurse is providing discharge teaching to a patient with chronic heart failure regarding daily weight monitoring at home. Which weight change should the patient report to the health care provider promptly?
options: A weight gain of 1 kg or more in 24 hours, or 2 kg or more in 1 week
A weight loss of 0.5 kg over 48 hours after starting loop diuretic therapy
A weight difference of 0.3 kg between morning and evening scale readings
A gradual weight gain of 1.5 kg over a 1-month period during winter months
items.rationale: Patients with heart failure should weigh themselves at the same time every morning in similar clothing and notify their health care provider if they gain 1 kg or more in 24 hours or 2 kg or more in 1 week, as this indicates fluid retention and worsening heart failure.

items.prompt: Which underlying medical condition predisposes a patient to digoxin toxicity by delaying renal drug excretion, thereby requiring a lower digoxin dosage?
options: Hyperthyroidism or gestational diabetes
Hypothyroidism or chronic kidney impairment
Iron-deficiency anemia or osteoarthritis
Seasonal allergic rhinitis or asthma
items.rationale: Digoxin is excreted via the kidneys. Patients with hypothyroidism, respiratory disease, kidney disease, or advanced age experience delayed renal drug excretion and require lower digoxin dosages to prevent toxicity.

items.prompt: A patient with heart failure is undergoing rapid intravenous digitalization in the intensive care unit. How does rapid digitalization compare with slow oral digitalization?
options: Slow digitalization requires inpatient telemetry because toxicity occurs within minutes
Rapid digitalization is safer than oral loading and is used in outpatient clinics
Rapid digitalization gives faster onset in acute distress, but toxicity can appear quickly
Rapid digitalization uses a lower total loading dose and avoids serum potassium checks
items.rationale: Rapid digitalization is reserved for hospitalized patients in acute distress to achieve therapeutic levels quickly, requiring continuous cardiac monitoring because toxicities can appear rapidly due to high drug concentrations. Slow digitalization is safer and can be done on an outpatient basis with oral doses.

items.prompt: A patient taking oral digoxin is prescribed cholestyramine for hyperlipidemia. How does cholestyramine interact with oral digoxin?
options: It inhibits hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and prolongs digoxin's elimination half-life
It competes for renal tubular secretion and increases serum digoxin levels by 50%
It displaces digoxin from plasma albumin binding sites and precipitates acute toxicity
It binds digoxin in the gastrointestinal tract and decreases its oral absorption
items.rationale: Cholestyramine, colestipol, and sucralfate decrease the oral absorption of digoxin in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to reduced therapeutic effect.

items.prompt: The nurse is reviewing serum digoxin levels for two patients: Patient A has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction in normal sinus rhythm, and Patient B has rapid atrial fibrillation. According to the textbook and Canadian guidelines, how do their target serum digoxin ranges compare?
options: Heart failure targets a lower range (0.5–0.9 ng/mL) than atrial fibrillation (0.8–1.5 ng/mL)
Heart failure requires higher levels (1.5–2.4 ng/mL) than atrial fibrillation (0.5–0.8 ng/mL)
Both conditions share an identical therapeutic target range of 1.2 to 2.2 ng/mL in adults
Atrial fibrillation requires subtherapeutic levels below 0.5 ng/mL to prevent heart block
items.rationale: For heart failure management, the Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines recommend lower target serum digoxin levels of 0.5–0.9 ng/mL (normal range 0.5–1 ng/mL or 0.8–2 ng/mL), whereas higher targets (0.8–1.5 ng/mL) are often needed to control ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation. Levels > 2.4 ng/mL often precipitate toxicity.

items.prompt: In which cardiac condition is digoxin contraindicated because it can paradoxically increase the ventricular rate?
options: Sinus tachycardia secondary to systolic dysfunction
Ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response
Paroxysmal atrial flutter with left ventricular dilation
items.rationale: Digoxin is contraindicated in ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation; in ventricular fibrillation, digoxin use may actually increase the ventricular rate. Other contraindications include hypersensitivity, second- or third-degree AV block, and subaortic stenosis.

items.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient with right ventricular heart failure. Which cluster of clinical findings is most consistent with right-sided heart failure rather than left-sided heart failure?
options: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, dry hacking cough, and resting hypoxemia
Bibasilar pulmonary crackles, orthopnea, tachypnea, and pink frothy sputum
Jugular venous distension, dependent pedal edema, ascites, and hepatic congestion
Exertional dyspnea, pleural effusions, S3 gallop, and pulmonary venous engorgement
items.rationale: Right ventricular heart failure causes increased hydrostatic pressure in the systemic venous circulation, leading to systemic venous congestion, jugular venous distension (JVD), pedal edema, ascites, and hepatic congestion. Left-sided heart failure causes pulmonary congestion ('left equals lung').

items.prompt: A patient with chronic hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy is diagnosed with heart failure due to diastolic dysfunction. Why are positive inotropic drugs like digoxin and milrinone generally avoided in isolated diastolic dysfunction?
options: Inotropic drugs accelerate adverse left atrial dilation and cause mitral valve prolapse
Positive inotropes selectively constrict the efferent renal arterioles in hypertensive patients
Diastolic dysfunction impairs sinoatrial node automaticity rather than myocardial relaxation
The primary defect is impaired ventricular relaxation and filling rather than weak contraction
items.rationale: Diastolic dysfunction involves a stiff ventricle that cannot relax and fill normally during diastole (often secondary to left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic hypertension). Positive inotropes (digoxin, milrinone) increase contraction force and are not the drugs of choice for diastolic failure; diuretics are used for symptom relief in both types.

items.prompt: A patient with heart failure is prescribed oral digoxin and intravenous calcium gluconate. Why must the nurse monitor this patient with caution?
options: Hypercalcemia increases cardiac irritability and the risk of digoxin-induced dysrhythmias
Parenteral calcium chelates circulating digoxin and neutralizes its positive inotropic action
Calcium competes with digoxin at renal tubules and doubles its urinary excretion rate
Elevated serum calcium blocks vagal stimulation and causes refractory sinus tachycardia
items.rationale: Parenteral calcium and hypercalcemia increase cardiac irritability in patients taking digoxin, placing them at higher risk for digoxin toxicity, sinus bradycardia, dysrhythmias, and heart block.

items.topic: Heart failure: Evaluation of heart failure therapy
items.prompt: A nurse is evaluating a patient 48 hours after initiating guideline-directed pharmacotherapy for acute heart failure. Which assessment finding best indicates a therapeutic response to the medications?
options: Weight gain of 1.2 kg over 24 hours with a resting heart rate of 112 beats/min
Increased urinary output, decreased lung crackles, and stronger peripheral pulses
Auscultation of a new S3 ventricular gallop with cool, pale lower extremities
Urine output of 20 mL/hr accompanied by orthopnea and jugular venous distension
items.rationale: Therapeutic effects of heart failure medications include increased urinary output (diuresis), decreased peripheral edema, decreased dyspnea and pulmonary crackles, reduced fatigue, resolution of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and warm, pink extremities with strong peripheral pulses.

items.prompt: What is the generic name of the specific antibody antidote used to reverse life-threatening digoxin toxicity?
items.rationale: Digoxin immune Fab (Digifab) is an ovine immunoglobulin fragment antibody that binds free digoxin into an inactive antigen–antibody complex to reverse life-threatening cardiotoxicity and hyperkalemia.

items.prompt: What is the generic name of the only currently available phosphodiesterase type III inhibitor (inodilator) used for short-term intravenous management of acute heart failure?
items.rationale: Milrinone (milrinone lactate) is the only phosphodiesterase inhibitor currently available for acute heart failure after the discontinuation of inamrinone.

items.prompt: What pharmacological term describes drugs that affect the force or energy of myocardial contractions?
items.rationale: Inotropic drugs affect the force or energy of myocardial contractions (positive inotropes increase contractility; negative inotropes decrease contractility). Chronotropic drugs affect heart rate, and dromotropic drugs affect electrical conduction velocity.

items.prompt: What is the generic name of the loop diuretic that must NEVER be injected into an intravenous line containing milrinone because it causes immediate chemical precipitation?
items.rationale: Furosemide precipitates upon contact with milrinone in intravenous lines and must be administered through a separate line.

items.prompt: Deficiency of which primary serum electrolyte (commonly depleted by loop diuretics) most strongly predisposes a patient to digoxin toxicity and serious dysrhythmias?
items.rationale: Low serum potassium (hypokalemia) enhances digoxin binding to the sodium–potassium ATPase pump, markedly increasing the risk of digoxin toxicity and life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmias.

items.prompt: What is the generic name of the beta-1-selective vasoactive adrenergic drug given by continuous intravenous infusion to increase contractility in patients with acute decompensated heart failure who are hemodynamically unstable?
items.rationale: Dobutamine (dobutamine hydrochloride) stimulates beta-1 receptors on the myocardium to produce a positive inotropic effect and increase stroke volume in hemodynamically unstable acute decompensated heart failure.

items.prompt: Accumulation of which insoluble peptide by-product in the bronchial tubes is responsible for the annoying dry cough associated with ACE inhibitors like lisinopril?
items.rationale: ACE inhibitors block the breakdown of bradykinins, which build up in the blood and lodge in the bronchial tubes, triggering a dry cough as the body attempts to expel them.

items.prompt: What two-word physiological term defines the proportion of blood ejected during each ventricular contraction compared with the total ventricular filling volume (normally about 65%)?
items.rationale: The ejection fraction is the proportion of blood ejected from the ventricle with each contraction relative to the left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV); normal is approximately 65% (0.65).

items.title: Digoxin Toxicity and Antidote Management in an Older Adult
items.topic: Heart failure: Cardiac glycosides and antidote
items.scenario: Arthur Pendelton, a 79-year-old man with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 32%) and atrial fibrillation, is brought to the emergency department by his daughter. Over the past 3 days, Arthur has had viral gastroenteritis with frequent watery diarrhea and poor oral intake. His home medications include lisinopril 10 mg PO daily, furosemide 40 mg PO twice daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg PO twice daily, and digoxin 0.25 mg PO daily. This morning, Arthur told his daughter that he feels dizzy, has no appetite, and everything in the kitchen looks 'tinted yellow with fuzzy halos around the ceiling lights.'

question.prompt: The nurse performs an initial assessment on Arthur. His blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 18 breaths/min, and his 0800 dose of digoxin is due now. When the nurse auscultates his apical pulse for 1 full minute, the rate is 46 beats/min and irregular. What is the nurse's priority action?
options: Give half of the 0.25-mg digoxin tablet and recheck his apical pulse in 1 hour
Administer the digoxin with an antiemetic and obtain a 12-lead ECG at noon
Withhold the digoxin dose, initiate continuous ECG monitoring, and notify the provider
Administer his scheduled carvedilol and furosemide first, then reassess his pulse
question.rationale: Arthur is exhibiting classic clinical manifestations of digoxin toxicity (bradycardia with apical pulse < 60 beats/min, anorexia, dizziness, and yellow halo vision) precipitated by dehydration and gastrointestinal losses. The nurse must withhold digoxin, initiate continuous ECG monitoring, and notify the prescriber.

stages.update: The nurse withholds the digoxin and places Arthur on a cardiac monitor, which reveals second-degree atrioventricular (AV) block with frequent premature ventricular contractions. Statutory blood work returns: serum digoxin 3.1 ng/mL, serum potassium 2.8 mmol/L, serum magnesium 0.62 mmol/L, and serum creatinine 168 µmol/L (baseline 95 µmol/L).

question.prompt: Which combination of factors in Arthur's history and laboratory findings directly precipitated his severe digoxin toxicity?
options: Reduced gastrointestinal digoxin absorption secondary to rapid intestinal transit
Hypercalcemia and hypernatremia induced by concurrent ACE inhibitor and beta blocker use
Impaired hepatic cytochrome P450 metabolism of digoxin triggered by viral illness
Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and acute kidney injury from dehydration and furosemide
question.rationale: Digoxin is excreted via the kidneys; dehydration and declining kidney function (creatinine 168 µmol/L) caused digoxin accumulation (3.1 ng/mL; toxic > 2.4 ng/mL). Simultaneously, diarrhea and furosemide caused hypokalemia (2.8 mmol/L) and hypomagnesemia (0.62 mmol/L), which sensitize the myocardium to digoxin toxicity and dysrhythmias.

stages.update: While intravenous potassium and magnesium replacement is being prepared, Arthur's cardiac rhythm deteriorates into sustained ventricular tachycardia with a blood pressure of 68/40 mm Hg, and he becomes unresponsive to verbal stimuli. The health care provider orders administration of the specific antidote for digoxin overdose.

question.prompt: What is the generic name of the antidote the nurse will prepare and administer intravenously to reverse Arthur's life-threatening digoxin cardiotoxicity?
question.rationale: Digoxin immune Fab (Digifab) is indicated for life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmias (such as sustained ventricular tachycardia or severe heart block) caused by digoxin toxicity. It binds free digoxin into an antigen–antibody complex.

stages.update: Arthur receives intravenous digoxin immune Fab and converts back to a stable rhythm with a heart rate of 68 beats/min and blood pressure of 114/70 mm Hg. Six hours later, the evening nurse notes a newly drawn total serum digoxin level of 8.4 ng/mL and a serum potassium level of 3.3 mmol/L.

question.prompt: Which nursing action is appropriate during the post-reversal monitoring phase following digoxin immune Fab administration?
options: Monitor clinical signs, ECG, and potassium levels, as total digoxin assays stay elevated
Administer a repeat dose of digoxin immune Fab because the digoxin level rose to 8.4 ng/mL
Give oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate to prevent rebound hyperkalemia after antidote therapy
Restart oral digoxin at 0.125 mg daily now that his sinus rhythm and blood pressure are stable
question.rationale: After digoxin immune Fab is given, total serum digoxin assays measure both bound and free digoxin and remain elevated for days to weeks; thus, clinical findings and ECG—not serum digoxin levels—guide monitoring. Additionally, as Na+/K+ ATPase pump function is restored, potassium shifts back into cells, requiring close monitoring for hypokalemia (muscle weakness, cramping, irregular rhythms).

items.title: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure and Milrinone Infusion in the ICU
items.scenario: Evelyn Bouchard, a 66-year-old woman with severe systolic heart failure (LVEF 22%, NYHA Class IV), is admitted to the intensive care unit with acute pulmonary edema and low cardiac output. She weighs 60 kg. Her blood pressure is 106/68 mm Hg, heart rate is 108 beats/min, respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min with bibasilar crackles, and SpO2 is 89% on 4 L/min nasal prongs. The intensivist prescribes a milrinone intravenous loading dose of 50 mcg/kg followed by a continuous infusion at 0.5 mcg/kg/min.

question.prompt: Based on Evelyn's weight of 60 kg and the prescribed loading dose of 50 mcg/kg, how many milligrams (mg) of milrinone should the nurse administer for the loading dose? (Enter the number only, e.g., 5)
question.rationale: Loading dose = 50 mcg/kg × 60 kg = 3 000 mcg. Converting micrograms to milligrams: 3 000 mcg ÷ 1 000 = 3 mg.

stages.update: The milrinone loading dose is completed and the continuous infusion is running via an infusion pump through Evelyn's right internal jugular central venous catheter. Thirty minutes later, the intensivist prescribes furosemide 40 mg IV × 1 dose now to relieve her pulmonary congestion.

question.prompt: How must the nurse administer the intravenous furosemide to ensure patient safety?
options: Inject the furosemide slowly into the proximal Y-port of the milrinone infusion line
Administer the furosemide via a separate IV line to prevent chemical precipitation
Dilute the furosemide in the milrinone infusion bag to provide continuous diuresis
Hold the milrinone infusion for 5 minutes while pushing furosemide through the lumen
question.rationale: Furosemide must not be injected into an intravenous line containing milrinone because a chemical precipitate forms on contact. The nurse must use a separate dedicated IV line or lumen.

stages.update: Four hours after starting the milrinone infusion and receiving IV furosemide, Evelyn's urine output has been 950 mL. Her cardiac monitor begins alarming with runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (6 to 8 beats), and her blood pressure drops to 80/46 mm Hg.

question.prompt: What is the nurse's priority action in response to Evelyn's hypotension and ventricular dysrhythmia?
options: Administer intravenous digoxin immune Fab to neutralize the circulating milrinone
Increase the milrinone infusion to 0.75 mcg/kg/min to augment systemic blood pressure
Reduce or temporarily stop the milrinone infusion and notify the prescriber promptly
Administer intravenous metoprolol to suppress the ectopy while continuing milrinone
question.rationale: Ventricular dysrhythmias (occurring in ~12% of patients) and hypotension secondary to vasodilation (especially when combined with diuretic-induced hypovolemia) are major adverse effects of milrinone. Because there is no specific antidote, the nurse should reduce or temporarily stop the infusion and contact the prescriber.

stages.update: The milrinone rate is reduced, normal saline bolus is given cautiously, and stat blood work is drawn. Results show: serum potassium 3.0 mmol/L, platelets 92 × 10^9/L (down from 185 × 10^9/L on admission), AST 68 U/L, and ALT 74 U/L.

question.prompt: Which statement accurately explains the laboratory abnormalities observed during Evelyn's milrinone therapy?
options: Low platelets and elevated transaminases indicate an acute allergic reaction to sheep protein
Milrinone causes pseudothrombocytopenia and hyperkalemia by binding to EDTA collection tubes
Elevated transaminases and low potassium are expected therapeutic markers of cAMP inhibition
Milrinone and loop diuretics cause hypokalemia, and milrinone can cause thrombocytopenia
question.rationale: Adverse effects of milrinone include ventricular dysrhythmias, hypotension, hypokalemia (worsened by concurrent loop diuretics), thrombocytopenia, headache, tremor, and elevated liver enzyme levels. Hypokalemia must be reported and corrected promptly to reduce dysrhythmia risk.

items.title: First-Line Heart Failure Pharmacotherapy and Managing ACE Inhibitor Cough
items.topic: Heart failure: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, and aldosterone antagonists
items.scenario: Adeep Dhaliwal, a 61-year-old accountant with a history of anterior myocardial infarction and hypertension, is diagnosed with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 36%, NYHA Class II). He reports fatigue and shortness of breath when climbing a flight of stairs. His vital signs are BP 138/86 mm Hg, HR 84 beats/min, and RR 16 breaths/min. Baseline labs show serum potassium 4.3 mmol/L and serum creatinine 88 µmol/L. The cardiologist initiates lisinopril 5 mg PO daily, metoprolol tartrate 25 mg PO twice daily, and furosemide 20 mg PO daily.

question.prompt: Adeep asks why he is being started on lisinopril and metoprolol first instead of digoxin, which his father took for heart failure years ago. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: ACE inhibitors and beta blockers slow remodeling and reduce mortality, whereas digoxin is an adjunct
Digoxin is reserved for acute inpatient pulmonary edema and is rarely prescribed for outpatient care
Lisinopril and metoprolol act as positive inotropes that directly increase intracellular calcium levels
Beta blockers and ACE inhibitors reverse systolic dysfunction within 6 months so therapy can stop
question.rationale: According to the 2017 Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines, ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril) and beta blockers (e.g., metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol) are the drugs of choice at the start of therapy to delay or reverse adverse left ventricular remodeling and reduce mortality. Digoxin does not reduce mortality and is reserved as an adjunct if moderate-to-severe symptoms persist.

stages.update: Three weeks later, Adeep returns to the heart failure clinic. His blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg, heart rate is 68 beats/min, his ankle edema has resolved, and his weight is stable. However, he reports a persistent, dry, hacking cough that keeps him awake at night. His lungs are clear to auscultation, and he is afebrile.

question.prompt: How should the nurse interpret Adeep's dry cough and anticipate changes to his medication regimen?
options: Refer him to the emergency department to rule out acute decompensated pulmonary edema
Explain that lisinopril causes a bradykinin cough and anticipate switching to valsartan
Advise him to hold his metoprolol dose because beta-1 blockade causes bronchial irritation
Instruct him to double his daily furosemide dose to clear subclinical alveolar fluid
question.rationale: ACE inhibitors like lisinopril commonly cause a dry, nonproductive cough due to accumulation of insoluble bradykinins in the bronchial tubes. In the absence of fluid overload (clear lungs, stable weight), the nurse should reassure the patient and contact the prescriber to consider switching to an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) such as valsartan.

stages.update: Adeep is switched from lisinopril to valsartan 80 mg PO twice daily, and his dry cough resolves. One year later, his heart failure progresses to NYHA Class III, and the cardiologist adds spironolactone 25 mg PO daily and recommends an over-the-counter adjunctive natural health product endorsed by Canadian guidelines.

question.prompt: Now that spironolactone has been added to Adeep's regimen with valsartan, which laboratory value and dietary teaching require priority nursing attention?
options: Check serum digoxin troughs weekly because spironolactone cross-reacts with valsartan
Encourage daily potassium supplements and bananas to prevent aldosterone-induced hypokalemia
Monitor serum potassium for hyperkalemia and caution against potassium supplements
Instruct him to take spironolactone with dairy products within 1 hour of his other medications
question.rationale: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist and potassium-sparing diuretic. Combining it with an ARB (valsartan) or ACE inhibitor increases the risk of hyperkalemia; therefore, serum potassium and kidney function must be monitored closely, and potassium supplements should be avoided unless specifically ordered.

stages.update: Adeep asks the nurse for the name of the natural health product supplement that the cardiologist recommended (1 g daily containing EPA and DHA ethyl esters) to help reduce his risk of hospitalization and mortality.

question.prompt: Which natural health product is recommended by the 2017 Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines as adjunctive therapy for patients with chronic heart failure?
question.rationale: The 2017 Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines recommend omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs, 1 g daily containing 850–882 mg of EPA and DHA as ethyl esters in a 1:1.2 ratio) as adjunctive therapy to reduce mortality and hospitalizations in chronic heart failure.

items.title: Pediatric Heart Failure and Safe Digoxin Administration
items.topic: Heart failure: Pediatric heart failure and cardiac glycosides
items.scenario: Maya Lin, an 8-month-old infant weighing 8 kg, is admitted to the pediatric cardiology unit with heart failure secondary to a large ventricular septal defect. Her parents report that she tires quickly during breast- and bottle-feeding, sweats profusely on her forehead while nursing, has poor weight gain, and breathes rapidly. On examination, her apical heart rate is 162 beats/min, respiratory rate is 58 breaths/min, and fine crackles are auscultated at the lung bases. The pediatric cardiologist orders oral furosemide and an oral digoxin digitalizing regimen of 30 mcg/kg PO divided into 3 equal doses over 24 hours.

question.prompt: Maya weighs 8 kg and the total oral digitalizing dose is 30 mcg/kg divided into 3 equal doses. How many micrograms (mcg) of digoxin will the nurse administer for EACH single dose? (Enter the number only, e.g., 50)
question.rationale: Total digitalizing dose = 30 mcg/kg × 8 kg = 240 mcg. Divided into 3 equal doses: 240 mcg ÷ 3 = 80 mcg (0.08 mg) per dose.

stages.update: The pharmacy dispenses digoxin pediatric elixir (50 mcg/mL). While performing an independent double-check before the first 80-mcg (0.08-mg) dose, the nurse notices a colleague has drawn up 0.8 mg (16 mL) instead of 0.08 mg (1.6 mL) due to a misread decimal point.

question.prompt: Why is strict adherence to decimal point rules and independent double-checks essential when calculating and administering digoxin in pediatric patients?
options: Decimal errors are mainly a concern with intravenous infusions rather than oral elixirs
Infants clear digoxin rapidly through the liver, requiring frequent 10-fold dose adjustments
Oral digoxin elixir has low bioavailability unless diluted in a full bottle of infant formula
Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index, and a decimal placement error causes a 10-fold overdose
question.rationale: Digoxin has a very narrow therapeutic index. As highlighted in the textbook's Special Populations: Children and Preventing Medication Errors boxes, a one-decimal-point placement error results in a 10-fold dosage error (and omitting a leading zero can cause a 100-fold error), which can be fatal.

stages.update: Maya receives the correct 80-mcg doses and is transitioned to a daily maintenance dose of digoxin and furosemide. On day 4 of hospitalization, Maya refuses her morning bottle, vomits twice, and her apical heart rate drops to 78 beats/min (normal for an awake 8-month-old infant is 100–160 beats/min).

question.prompt: How should the nurse interpret Maya's new clinical findings?
options: Withhold the digoxin and notify the provider, as vomiting and bradycardia indicate toxicity
Document the heart rate of 78 beats/min as an expected therapeutic response to digitalization
Administer the digoxin with oral electrolyte solution and recheck her apical pulse in 2 hours
Give an extra dose of oral furosemide to relieve gastric venous congestion and stop the vomiting
question.rationale: In infants and children, digoxin toxicity is manifested by nausea, vomiting, anorexia (feeding refusal), bradycardia, and dysrhythmias. The nurse must withhold the digoxin and notify the health care provider.

stages.update: Maya's serum digoxin level is adjusted, her potassium is replenished, and she stabilizes for discharge prior to her scheduled surgical repair. The nurse is providing discharge education to Maya's parents.

question.prompt: Which statement by Maya's parents indicates an accurate understanding of home care and when to contact the health care provider?
options: If Maya vomits within 30 minutes of a digoxin dose, we will give a repeat dose right away.
We will call the doctor if Maya gains 1 kg in 24 hours, vomits, or has trouble breathing.
We will mix her digoxin elixir into a full bottle of milk so she can sip it over the afternoon.
Once Maya is feeding well without sweating next week, we can taper off her digoxin at home.
question.rationale: Parents should be taught to notify the health care provider if fatigue, sudden weight gain (1 kg or more in 24 hours), palpitations, tachycardia or bradycardia, vomiting, or respiratory distress develop or worsen. Doses should not be repeated or doubled without consulting the provider, and heart failure medications must not be stopped abruptly.

items.title: Progressive Heart Failure Management in a Black Patient
items.topic: Heart failure: Vasodilators, beta blockers, diuretics, and inotropes
items.scenario: Marcus Vance, a 58-year-old Black man with a history of hypertension and an anterior myocardial infarction 8 years ago, is hospitalized with worsening heart failure. He has been taking lisinopril, carvedilol, and oral furosemide 20 mg daily at home. To optimize his regimen, the cardiologist adds oral hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate.

question.prompt: After administering the first dose of hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate at 0800, what is the priority nursing assessment and safety intervention over the next 1 to 2 hours?
options: Maintain strict fluid restriction and prepare digoxin immune Fab in case tachycardia develops
Assess colour vision hourly for yellow-green halos as peak plasma levels are reached
Monitor blood pressure closely and assist with position changes due to the risk of syncope
Encourage brisk ambulation in the hallway 1 hour after dosing to evaluate exercise tolerance
question.rationale: Hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate are specifically recommended for Black patients with heart failure and achieve peak plasma levels in 1 hour. They must be used with caution—especially with the first few doses—because of the risk of hypotension and syncope. If syncope occurs, the drug is usually discontinued.

stages.update: On hospital day 3 during morning rounds, Marcus becomes restless and dyspneic. His heart rate increases to 122 beats/min, his weight has increased from 78 kg to 80 kg over the past 2 shifts, he has 3+ bilateral ankle and lower leg edema, bibasilar lung crackles are audible, and his SpO2 drops from 97% to 87% on room air. The prescriber orders oxygen at 2 L/min via nasal prongs to keep SpO2 > 90%, furosemide 20 mg IV stat, an increase in oral furosemide to 40 mg daily, and a nitroglycerin transdermal patch 0.4 mg/hr q12h (apply now and remove at night).

question.prompt: Why is the nitroglycerin transdermal patch ordered to be applied in the morning and removed at night (every 12 hours), and what is its therapeutic effect in acute heart failure?
options: Removing the patch at night allows nocturnal venous pooling to stimulate endogenous natriuresis
Nitroglycerin increases contractility via cAMP, and nighttime removal prevents ventricular ectopy
The transdermal reservoir is exhausted after 12 hours and causes rebound hypertension if kept on
Nitroglycerin dilates vessels to reduce preload, and a patch-free interval prevents tolerance
question.rationale: Transdermal nitroglycerin acts as a vasodilator in acute and chronic heart failure to decrease venous return (preload) and reduce the workload of the heart. Removing the patch at night provides a 10- to 12-hour nitrate-free interval to prevent tolerance.

stages.update: Despite oxygen, diuretics, and vasodilators, Marcus's condition worsens that evening into acute decompensated heart failure with hemodynamic instability: blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg, cool clammy extremities, weak peripheral pulses, and oliguria. He is transferred to the coronary care unit, and a continuous intravenous infusion of dobutamine is ordered.

question.prompt: Before and during the continuous intravenous infusion of dobutamine, which nursing assessment and understanding of the drug's mechanism is accurate?
options: Assess IV vein status closely and monitor for improved output from beta-1 receptor stimulation
Transition dobutamine to an oral tablet once blood pressure exceeds 100/60 mm Hg for 2 hours
Expect the heart rate to decrease below 55 beats/min due to dobutamine's negative chronotropic action
Infuse dobutamine through the same lumen as intravenous sodium bicarbonate to prevent phlebitis
question.rationale: Dobutamine hydrochloride is a beta-1-selective adrenergic agonist given by continuous intravenous infusion for hemodynamically unstable acute decompensated heart failure. Assessing the status of the patient's veins is essential, and therapeutic evaluation focuses on improved contractility, stroke volume, peripheral pulses, skin warmth, and urine output.

stages.update: After 3 days in the coronary care unit, Marcus is weaned off dobutamine, stabilized on oral guideline-directed therapy (including digoxin 0.125 mg PO daily added for persistent HFrEF symptoms), and prepared for discharge home.

question.prompt: Which statement by Marcus during discharge teaching indicates that he understands his home medication and self-care regimen?
options: If my radial pulse is below 60 or above 120 beats/min, I will take an extra half-tablet of digoxin.
I will weigh myself daily, check my pulse for 1 minute, and avoid bran or dairy near dosing times.
I will take my morning digoxin with wheat bran cereal and yogurt to prevent stomach irritation.
If I miss my morning digoxin by more than 12 hours, I will take two tablets the following morning.
question.rationale: Discharge teaching for heart failure includes measuring daily morning weights in similar clothing, checking the radial pulse for 1 full minute before digoxin (contacting the provider if < 60 bpm, erratic, or ≥ 120 bpm), not stopping medications abruptly, and avoiding antacids, dairy products (milk, ice cream, yogurt, cheese), or bran within 2 hours before or after oral heart failure medications.
